etonging to t,. are £4,837 for this year, and the widow's fund .... _ _ CANADA COMPARED WITTE UNITED STATES FOR DAIRY- ING —Over the United States, especially over the Western ones, Canada has the immense agricultural advantage of a summer rainfall, which prevents the land from being parched and scorched with excessive heat and drought. Wheat will ripen at latitude 58 deg., and barley at 65 deg., which is some three to four hundred milesnorth of the Ork- neys and Shetlands •, but this occurs only in the north-west of Canada; for in the north-east, in the direction of Hud- son's Bay, the Arctic currents that sweep down the coast of Labrador lower the temperature, and push further south the limits of grains and grasSes. But wherever wheat and bar- ley will ripen, in a climate whose summer rainfall can be depended on, there is a good prospect for grasses and roots, and greencroPs generally; and though the winters are severe, making the wintering of live-stock an arduous duty, they begin and leave off again with a regularity which enables the farmer to make nicer calculations than he can think of doing in the British Islands; and, as the frosts are keen, and last as a rule for a considerable period, the ground is mellowed and pulverised to a degree which greatly lessens the work of preparing it for the seed, while the gradual melting of the show in spring gives to the soil a supply of moisture which is of great service to the newly- germinated seeds. Over a considerable portion of the United States, west of St. Louis_west, that is, of the 98th meridian—the summer rainfall is altogether insufficient for the needs of vegetation. During four or five months of the year—and they the most important agricultural months —grasses cannot flourish, and roots and green-crops are out of the question; so that the vast district west of Illinois, reaching to the Pacific, is not adapted to dairying, and never can be, unless vast forests are planted to increase the rainfall, and irrigation works on a vast scale are carried out against wherever water for the purpose may he had. All this tells whichsi on of :rlomu leddean otherwise da i r;vhi navge re been thepos slm almost unlimited the expansion . and Canada promises at no distant period of the world's history to become almost as great a stock-raising and dairy- ing country as its neighbour the United States—pursuits for which its Soil, climate, and general characteristics appear to be eminently suitable. The soil and climate of Canada, in fact, throughout the vast area, are favourable to the growth of many useful pasture and forage grasses, and the country in general is well watered, while both the luad and labour are cheaper, and taxation lighter, than in the United States. —.Dairy Farming. THE Any OF GRAFTING.—Now there is one subject upon I which a few words may just at this time be aptly said with advantage, but upon which, as far as we are aware, we have hitherto kept sileace, and that is the method and process of grafting. And not only is our subject an interesting, in- structive, and important one, but it is, as we well know, venerable and time-honoared. St. Paul, we recollect, freely illustrated from grafting, while, nearly 400 years before, 1 Demosthenes adverted to it; Plutarch and Pliny alike men- I tion it, although the latter would seem to have had hut an imperfect knoerledge of the principles of grafting, since he assigns as a reason of the production of some apples that I were of an unusually rosy red, that originally they had I been grafted upon a mulberry stock; whereas we know that 1 our stock, or wild tree, in no sense affects the piece that we graft upon it, least of all does it colour the fruit ! The stock, in fact, merely supplie,i nourishment, and that is all. be asked, What object is there in the Now it may probably system of grafting? What advantages do we gain by it? They are -1-11nv, as we shall presently see. If we depended merely fir the increase of our garden supply upon cuttings, we should be in a sorry plight, for it would be years before any subject raised from a cutting, could be of any practical use ; whereas, probably , the self.same cutting, if grafted successfully upon a sturdy and healthy stock, might in a couple of year's time result in a tree. Our first advantage, then, from the system of grafting is that the entire strength of the stock is thrown into that which is grafted upon it. And next, we are by this means evidently able to increase any choice class of fruit with comparatively no difficulty, av a piece with a single bud upon it is sufficient for a graft, if a promising one. Then again, when we have ascertained what are the growing properties of OUT stock, that is to say. whether it is very vigorous or not, we can either increase our of any more delicate kind, or reduce that of the . of an v species of fruit that we are wishing to pro- pagate, simply by grafting our delicate sorts upon vigorous stocks, and our rapidly mowing or vigorous cuttings upon our less vigorous stocks. The cutting, or piece, that We graft upon our stock Is commonly called the scion, appar- ently a word of French extraction, signifying a young twig qr shoot.—Cassell's Family Mayarine.

"I would much rather," observed Mr. E., it had been for a euit." flow TO SADDLE A COLT.—The better plan is to aCetle- tem the colt from a very early period to bear first a sur- cingle, then a pad, and then a dumb jockey, from which light stirrups and a skirt may by degrees be suspended, try- ing and accustoming him to each new thing thoroughly before another is introduced to his notice. Supposing that the colt has been led about in the lonveing-rein until accus- tomed to all ordinary sights and sounds, has learned to obey the breaker, and has become so muck accustomed to him that he will allow him, or any quiet person, to approach him oc either side without starting back affrighted—that he has, in fact, learned that man is both his friend and his master— a saddle may then be placed on his back.—The Book of the Horse. CARLYLE'S INFLUENCE ON THE POLITICAL HISTORY OF His TlME.—Carlyle has exerted, I think, a very potent in- fluence on the political history of our day—more. however, through the power of his imaginative picture of the tur- bulent fermentations and molten fury of popular democracy than by his attempt to persuade the peoples to give up " palavers," " ballotings," dm., and to let wise men guide them and rule them. Such books as his "Chartism," "Past and Present," "Latter Day Pamphlets," in spite of all their humour and all their various truth of insight— which was not small—did little if anything to influence the popular mind. And as to his apologies for slavery, and his vehement attacks on "Black Quashes," they were so utterly , inconsistent with the drift of the known facts of the case, , and contained practical advice so malign in its tendency, not only to the slaves but to the slave-owners, that I think I they altogether failed, in this country at least, of political effect. But his wonderful and unique picture of a democ- racy stirred to its depths, in "The French Revolution," produced a profound impression of warning, and partly even of terror, on those who could understand it; and through them the impression spread to many, so that the dangers of democracy have been more fully appreciated ever since, and will be the better understood for all time to come in consequence of Carlyle's marvellous picture.—R. H. Hutton, in Good Words. NEW me ENTOMOLOGY.—As Mr. Jones was returning from a party with his family he discovered a new and singular loouing insect on his front door step. As he is something of a scientist, he was naturally pleased with the new speci- men, and, forming his pocket handkerchief into a cage, he pounced down upon it, and succeeded in capturing it. "Bring the microscope, children," he said, "and tell your ma to hurry ; I want her to look at it. I'm sure it belongs to the Hemiptera class, and is a new specimen. Here, Charlie, put your eye to the ocular side and tell me what you see." "Oh, pa, ain't it splendid? It's got four wings, eight Ayes, and oh, my! ain't it a sparkler, though? Red, and green, and yellow, and oh! it is getting away, ain't it, pa?" "Then it isn't dead !" cried Mr. Jones, in ecstacy ; ,"I wasn't quite sure whether it moved or not. Let me look. Yes, it's a terrestrial, I think, after all; it belongs to the genus Pentatoma—the antennse have that peculiar flexible look; and yet, now that I look again, the eyes seem to indicate that it is a phytocols, in which case it will be very destructive to your ma's plants, and we must kill it at I once. I'll ask Professor Sill. It will be, in any case, a valuable addition to science. Maria where's the chloro- form ?" "Up on the clock-shelf. What are you going to do with it ?' asked Mrs. Jones, who had been giving her un- divided attention to the baby. " Kill this bug as soon as you have examined it," answered Mr. Jones in a lofty tone. " I shall present it to the "Detroit Scientific Association—" "Well, I guess not, Mr. Jones," broke in his wife, who was looking with much interest at the new specimen, "I paid 2 dole, for that bug last week to wear on my new bonnet, and I must have dropped it off when I came in. It belongs to the genuine millinerve, and couldn't be any deader if it had been baked for a century. Science will have to get along without it, Jones; it's already classified." Poor Jones!— Detroit Free Press.

1 • - , lien of finer or more numerous . :s. ion this point are, however, much to be desired. 1 The production of tubers in which is stored up nourish- meat for a future generation of plants enables the potato to perpetuate its race in a way much more effective than in this particular plant could be secured by the seed. In its native country the roots and haulms perish at the end of the season just as they do with us. But there the tubers remain buried in a dry soil, while in this country the soil is not only damp, but frequently quite wet all through the winter, so that if left in the soil here the tuber might either sprout too soon or rot away altogether; the variations of temperature between warm winter days and sharp frosty ones would also be inimical to the health of the tubers. It appears on the face of it, therefore, that autumn sowing of potatoes is hardly likely to succeed in this country, but that as heretofore spring sowing will continue to be the practice. There is no more delicate farm crop than the potato, and a May frost will usually find out the weak point that betrays the sub-tropical origin of the plant, and oftentimes leads to a serious injury, which makes itself felt in the pocket of the grower. The terrible disease to which it falls so easy a pres is not uncommonly encouraged by the practice of put- ting too much farmyard manure on the land, because it pro- motes a rank growth of tops. We are aware that the Lothian farmers put as much farmyard dung as they can on potato lands, but they do it with their eyes open, and with full knowledge of the danger, for they think the risk of get- ting disease is worth running, because of the very large crops which are obtained when plenty of dung is used. Potatoes require a good deal of potash, and in soils which do not contain enough of this ingredient no fertiliser is of so much value as kainit, a mineral obtained from Germany, and worth about 50s. a ton in London or Liverpool. The large quantities of French and Irish potatoes an- nually imported into England show that the acreage under this crop might with advantage be increased. Of all our so-called "vegetables," potatoes are by far the most valued and the most indispensable, and though they have only been known in Europe for about three centuries it is difficult to surmise how we should get on without theria.—Mark Lane

• - Tai RA.NSACICIFIG OF THE PYRAALIDS.—Under the Arab dominion the rulers themselves undertook this task, by no means a light one; finding nothing but empty sarcophagi and bodies, they endeavoured to justify themselves in the eyes of their subjects for the sums they had squandered, and spread the false intelligence that they had found exactly as mach gold as the work of opening the tombs had cost. When the labourers under Mamoon (died A.D. 813), the son of Haroun el Rasheed, who is so will known to every reader of the " Arabian Nights," had penetrated to the heart of the Pyramid of Cheops, it is said that they sound a treasure, and also a marble tablet on which were these words "Such a King, son of such a King, in such year will open this pyramid, and spend a certain sum of money in so doing. We here repay him for his undertaking ; but if he persists in his enterprise, be will sacrifice much money and gain no- thing." In fact, searching the Pyramids has enriched no one; and though we hear romantic tales of thins said to have been found there, yet, on the whole, ransacking a pyra- mid has been generally regarded as a crime, to be followed by retribution, or even by death.—Egypt : Descriptive, His. toricat, and Picturesque.

LINES ON MY WIFE'S FIF IY-NINTH BIRTHDAY. Tho' all the ups and downs of life, And many we have had together. There's none like thee I call my wife. In sunshine or in wintry weather. Thy name I changed at twenty-four. When in the bloom of youth and beauty. And ever since those days of yore Affection thrives with daily duty. My joys you've doubled, sorrows have divided, And soothed the troubles of many years; save lightened heavy cares which hayed subsided. And wiped from misery's eyes the bitter tears. ISay life to thee be lengthened over long. Its path be strewed with all the choicest flowers ; Years fifty-nine, the burden of my song, The month of April cold, without its showers. King's Clough, 4th April, 1891. J. C. B.

-- - Written on seeing a child at play, while I was undergoing a season of trouble.
The cloud of trouble, blask and drear, Hung o'er my head In threatening guise; A sweet young child did then appear, To cheer my heart,—and dry my eyes. *

Sweet prattler, with thine eves of blue. Th n playest on the stage of life •, Unconscious of the storms that brew In this wide world of woe and strife. Dow b. ight thy childhood's 81.111 la shining. Thy pathway one of ight and flowers. A thousand blessings thee entwining, And happy all thy golden hours. A mother's fond love, jealous ever Of ought that rob.. thee of thy bliss ; Efoly hard a task t'would be to sever Thy young h-art from a love like this. Each hour for thee is e'er unfolding, Something flea' from f tnev's store That pleases thee, one short hour holding Favour with thee,—but no more. Each !calk. each .mile, Pach word cementiug Thy mother's heart, in love to thee; And oh, how bitter her lamenting, If ought :like trouble near thee be. Dream on, sweet child, life's happy dreams, Enjoy pleasures. while you may: There comes a time; (how hard it seems), When childhood's dreams shall fade away. St. Helen's. J. G. PICKEesGin. - PANSIES. I send thee pansies while the year is young, Yellow as sunshine, purple as the night; Flowers of remembrance, ever fondly sung By all the chiefest of the Sons of Light; And if in recollection lives regret For Wasted days and dreams that were not true, I tell thee that the "pansy freak'd with jet" Is still the heart's-ease that the poets knew. Take all the sWeetness of a gift unsought, And for the pansies send me back a thought. —Good Words. SARAH DOUDNEY.

Corbieres, one of Louis Ministers, during an interview with the King, somewhat familiarly took out his snuff-box and handkerchief and placed them on the tablei "Have you quite finished einptying your pockets ?" asked Louis. "Sire," replied Corbieres," I err through excess of zeal. I empty my pockets instead of filling them at youi Majesty's expense." An American paper has arranged the following as a Emil rhyme for the months : January, sneezy; February, freery March. breezy; April, wheezy; May, showery ; Jane, lowery ; July, bowery; August, flowery; September, blowy ; October, ftowey ; November, snowey ; December, glowey. HANDLING PIGEONS.—We may just say a word on the proper way of handling or holding a pigeon. This is with the breast across the palm of the hand, the head towards the liftl fingsr or body of the holder. The legs should be al- lowed to page through between the first and second fingers, when the thumb can be brought over the back, and will hold the bird perfectly secure. In catching a pigeon, the best way, if possible, is to get the hand over the back, with the forefinger in front of the neck, and the thumb under the breast--Musfrated Book of Pigeons. A certain farmer in the county of Durham once bought some bone dust, to be pat on a field on his farm, but found fault as he had got no benefit with the same. The secret came out afterwards. ?be man in charge, to save himself the trouble of spreading the same, had emptied it all down an old pit shaft in the fields. AN ATTTACTIMENT.—A young bachelor sheriff was called upon to serve an attacnment against a beautiful young widow. He accordingly called for her, and said, "Madam, I have an attachment for you." The widow blushed, and said his attachment was reciptocated. "You don't under- stand me; you must proceed to court." "I know it is leap year, sir, but I prefer you to do the courting." "Mrs. P—, this is no time for trifling; the justice is waiting." • The justice is waiting! Why, I prefer a parson." An unknown disease, resulting already in the death of over 100 valuable animals, has broken out amongst the deek herds in the Duke of Portland's park at Welbeck, Notting- hamshire. More deer are dying daily, and at present no means have been found to stop the spread of the affection. A post-mortem examination ef one of the bodies has been made by Mr. Henry Moore, veterinary surgeon, of Work- sop, and he states that he found a small thread-like worm infesting the bronchial tubes of the lungs and small intes- tines, the irritation of which caused congestion and inflam- mation of both organs, the symptoms being aggravated by the late prolonged wet and severe weather. The parasites are white, no thicker than a hair, and lin. long. It is re- ported that similar disease has broken out in other English deer parks. A BIITCIE BABY SONG.—The following is a specimen of a Dutch baby song, which, although it is not in English, has such an easy and merry jingle that children in this country will have no trouble in reading it, and will possibly also understand it. There are only six lines altogether, and in Roman type they take this form:— Trip a trep a tronjes, De varkens in de boonjes. De keejes in de klaver, De pearden in de haver. De eenjes in de waterplass So groot myn klein was. Perhaps some reader acquainted with child life in Holland will be able to say whether this rhyme or anything like it is still in use among the families across the North Sea. The paper from which it Is taken states that in New York in the colonial days the grandpa or grandma trotted the youngster to the song of "Trip a tep." The meaning of the rhyme is that when the child climbs upon the knee of its parent or grandparent it is as happy as the little pigs among the beans the cows among the clover (de keejes in de klaver), the lunges among the oats, and the ducks splashing in the • water. At the last line the singer throws the baby up, pro- nouncing its name, whatever that may be, as ho does SO— '" so great my little was. 111614.` DIIOOIIXDA RECELVED ITS NAME. —ln herdic legends, ever the first heralds of history, we read of Heber and rieremon being opposed by the Magi or Druids at this spot, called Druidhechta in the record, whence the learned antiquarian, the late John D'Alton, conjectured the town derived its name. This, however, is but a conjecture, to be received with the greater hesitation as a more reliable origin i/3 assigned. At all events, long before the Christian era there arose upon the sloping banks of the Buvinda,or Boyne, on either side, where it runs eastward into the Irish Sea at Inver-Colpa, rude huts of wood or wickerwork, covered with fern or heath, the ahodes of men who lived by fishing or commerce with the opposite coast of Lancashire. To con- nect the northern _gad southern sides a rude bridge was thrown on piles across the spot where the river was ford- able. This was called Drohed-ath, the Bridge of the Ford, whence is derived the present name of Drogheda, which Ptolemy and early historians rendered into Latin as "Pens Vadi," or "Pontana Civitas," and the English into Droheda, Drohed, and Tredagh.—Our Own Country. A BENGALI'S APPRECIATION OF TIM BEAITITES OF BOB- SAY.—" A Bengali" writes to a Calcutta paper from "Cross- keys Hotel," Bombay :—He who ever wishes to enjoy the beauties of the Nadan Kanan in the paradise of Indra, may come to the seaside of Bombay, and take a walk on the streets just by the side of the Malabar Hills when the sun, after the labour of the whole day, sinks down the horizon, beautifying the sea and the sky with enchanting yellow colour; and his wishes will be fulfilled. There the deep blue water of the Arabian Sea strikes the shore of India with deep murmuring voice. As far ae. angels' ken" nothing is - there but watery expanse; the sky touches the sea and the sea the sky. Far, far on the sea, ships are going always like some sea birds. The naughty little waves are playing with the air on the breast of the sea, running hither and thither ; sometimes they come dashing towards the belch, and break into thousand white pieces, as if little boys at their play run towards their mothers' lap, and jumping into that abode of infancy, burst into anwelic laughter. The sun is half under the blue water and half above it, on the blue sky. The little Armenian, Jew, and Parsi girls with their beautiful black hair flowing on the back of their red or yellow petty coats, .--ye-qatxying-all around on the sea shore. Before you, as far as you can see, a blue wide sea, with the golden sun, half sunk under the beautiful water; above you the boundless blue sky, with golden clouds moving slowly on the evening air; , ereissianng up to the sky with d plants; around you behind you the wMiatlhabvaarriailislltsr, beautiful houses. the charming angels in fairy costumes, playing, walking, and dancing—you forget that you are in this world of misery, you think yourselves transported to that happy garden of god', so much sung by the poets. Stop, dear reader, stop here for this day. '1 shall show you;a11 the luties of this city of merchants, one after another.

aHE le._ the Liberation Society have considered Mr. Blennerhassett's Marriages Registration Bill, and have determined that "being based on erroneous principles, and being otherwise objectionable," it should be opposed. The influence of the society will therefore be used to throw out the bill on its second reading. Arrangements are being made for a Con- ference of Nonconformists, with the object of considering the laws regulating marriages in Dissenting places of wor- ship. The suggestion emanates from the Congregational Union. and has received the approval of the Executive Com- rnitte of the Liberation Society. The t tembers of the Yorkshire Congregational Union re- solved on Wednesday, at their meeting in Leeds, to express to the Government their warm appreciation "of the coura- geous sense of justice and Christian rectitude, as well as a desire to avoid needless bloodshed," 'displayed in the con- clusion of peace with the Transvaal Boers. The Union declined, however, to add to the resolution the expression of a hope that the Government will take steps to protect the natives of the Transvaal against the introduction of a system of slavery. The proposal was successfully objected to on the ground that the Union was not a political organi- sation. A branch of the East Somerset Liberal Association was inaugurated at Frome, on Wednesday. Mr. Samuelson, M.P., who was the chief speaker, urged the necessity for a reform in the present system of county government upon a thoroughly representative basis. Every ratepayer should be represented and have some one to speak for him. The ques- tion could only be adequately dealt with by such a states- man as Mr. Gladstone. To pass a bad bill would be worse than passing no bill at all. Farmers should agitate for the appointment of a Minister to leiok after agricultural affairs and who ought to have a seat in the Cabinet. 4,o:10 ANTI-RITOAL MEMORIAL TO THE PRIMATE.—A memo- rial, signed by 22,000 laymen, was presented to the Arch- bishop of Canterbury, on Saturday, in opposition to the claim recently made for "the recognised toleration of wide diversities of ceremonial" in the Church of England. The feeling which prompted the memorialists is described as one of profound uneasiness lest, under the plea of toleration, ceremonial practices and doctrines should obtain recogni- tion which are alien to the spirit of the Prayer Book. The signatories include, besides many members of both Houses of Parliament, 141 generals and other officers of the army, 31 admirals aud other officers of the navy, 79 pliyslcians and surgeons, 75 barristers and solicitors, and 191 magis- trates. On Monday, about midnight, another violent explosion took place at the Chatterley Coal and Iron Company's Whit- field golliery, the scene of the recent terrible disaster whereby 17 lives were lost. For the last eight or ten days workmen have been engaged placing air pipes in the down- cast shaft, and were expecting in a very short time to be able to enter the workings where the bodies of 15 poor fellows have lain since February 7th. It was thought that the fire was completely overcome by the filling in of the upcast shaft for nearly one hundred yards with earth and the turning down the other shaft of a stream of water for a lengthened period, but suddenly another explosion occurred, which was of so violent a nature as to blow out the air pipes, doing con- siderable damage to the head gears and machinery at the top of the shaft, and seriously injuring one of the men in charge of the operations. A NOBLE WORK.—In the April number of Little Folks Magazine the editor announces that the amount (£1,755 10s. dd.) subscribed by his readers, in response to the appeal made by him on behalf of the East London Hospital for Children at Shadwell, has been sufficient to permanently endow two cots in that institution, and that both cots are now open. From time to time it is Intended to give in the Magazine accounts of the various occupants of these two cots, under the title of "Stories of the Little Folks' Cots : and thus it is hoped that the interest already taken in these little patients will be maintained. In connection with t f his e noble work of befriending their poorer sisters and brothers who are suffering in our midst, with which the readersof Little Folks have specially identified themselv es. we are in- formed in the same number of the Magazine that another competition painting-book, called "The Little Folks, Illumi- nating Book "—all the copies of which are intended to be eventually distributed among the Children's Hospital—is nearly ready. For the best coloured comes of this book prizes in money, books, and medals are offered, and children of all ages up to IS are eligible to take part in the competi- tion. Ifew Seasons Marmalade now ready.—Hartley's Mb. jars."

LORD PALMERSTON. We have already seen tbat daring no less than 19 years Lord Palmerston filled the office of Secretary at War, re- peated change of Cabinet Ministers within the period not having affected hie position. But the chief phase a his official life opened in 1830 when he became Foreign Secre- tary—an office that he filled for 11 years with the exception of the five months of the Peel Ministry in 1834-5. His pre- fious apprenticeship had undoubtedly prepared him for this More responsible position, and when he accepted the seals of the office it was generally acknowledged that he was the tight man in the right place. In this capacity he won for himself a name all over Europe, and the cordial hatred of the despots of the Continent. And during that ten years' run of power which the Reform Bill gave to the Whigs, he stood forth as the most brilliant member of the Cabinet— the Man of Men—the Minister of Ministers—the type aid glory of England. His ambition was to make the influence of England felt everywhere, and there can be no doubt that he greatly increased the importance of the Foreign Office by his administration of its affairs, however rash and ob- jectionable may have been some of his despatches. The policy which Lord Palmerston pursued while at the Foreign Office has evei been a battle-ground for politiciaus. There were those who, regarding him as the "firebrand of Europe," a "luckless inciter match," an "English Jonah," always creating a storm round the Ship of State, were pro- pared to impeach his Lordship and hurl him in ignominy and shame from office. There were others who, looking on with unspeakable satisfaction as he humbled the Shah, patronised the Sultan, abolished the Mogul, conquered the Brother of the Sun, and opened to the world the empire which had been walled round for centuries by impregnable barriers, shouted themselves hoarse in praising Lord Palmerston as the beat of all Foreign Ministers. The exponents of England's Foreign Po' icy have gene- rally been divided into two classes, viz., the advocates of the policy of interference and the advocates of the policy of non-resistance. Our late Prime Minister, with his bastard Imperialism and pinchbeck glory, belongs to the first class, while Lord Aberdeen belonged to the latter. But Palmer- ston insisted upon it that there was a middle course be- tween interference and absolute silence. In the first great speech on "Our Foreign Relations" which Lord Palmerston delivered (June 11th, 1829) in Opposition, and which marked him out as the future Foreign Secretary, he laid down principles which afford the key to his subsequent con- duct in office:—"There are two great parties in Europe—one which endeavours to bear sway by the force of public opinion; another which endeavours to bear sway by the force of physical control; and the judgment, almost unani- mous, of Europe assigns the latter as the present connection of England. The principle on which the system of this party is founded is in my view fundamentally erroneous. There is in nature no moving power but mind; all else is passive and inert. In human affairs this power is opinion ; in political affairs it is public opinion; and: he who can, grasp the power, with it will subdue the fleshly arm of phy- sical strength and compel it to work out his purpose." This was the weapon of weapons. Lord Palmerston had faith in its power. He believed also in the right of every man to have this weapon at his side and to use it as he could, but if this weapon,failed then he ranged himself definitely with those who had but the one resource of brute power—thesne baptism of blood and fire. Without endorsing these opinions to the full, we cannot but feel that there is something noble in such a view of na- tional duties and that it certainly was the conception on which Lord 'Palmerston acted. After all, the best vindica- tion of the Minister from the charges against his policy on the ground that it was intermeddling and high-handed is to be found in the fact that it accomplished its ends and ac- complished them for the most part by pacific means. It is to be remembered to his credit that England has seldom held a more proud position than under his Administration, and that the one great war into which we have been dragged during the last forty years was brought on by the drifting policy of Lord Aberdeen, and not by the decided and manly statesmanship which was characteristic of Lord Palmerston. Our space will not allow us to discuss his policy in de- tail, but we may refer to one or more of his brilliant achievements while Secretary for Foreign Affairs. Fere- most among the results of Lord Palmerston's policy must be mentioned the establishment of Belgium as an inde- pendent kingdom with a free Constitution. When Lard Palmerston assumed the seals of office the spirit of Revolu- tion was in the air. On every hand crowns were falling into the gutter. The Insurrection by which we were most affected was the Belgian one. We had sufficiently learnt the danger and the cost of having to watch and defend our- , selves against an enemy possessing the long line of coast by, which we had been hostilely confronted during the reign.. of Napoleon. At his fall we took precautions against being exposed to similar dangers, and our main object at the Con- ° gress of Vienna was to guard the Netherlands from future invasion. We bad imagined that we had done so by uniting Holland and Belgium hoping thus to have created a power- ful kingdom, of which we had protected the frontier by fortresses raised under our inspection and, in some degree, at our expense. But the fall of the Bourbon throne in France—the triumph of the citizens and the Press against the soldiery of Charles X.—was the signal for the Belgians to rise against an arbitrary and unpopular Sovereign. Lord Palmerston at once saw the dangers ahead, and set himself to avert them. Here, as everywhere, he sought to mediate ' between extremes, and yet to secure that constitutional liberty in which he believed the true security of nations lay. He set his face against ambitious schemes wherever entertained, and, having no idea of claiming special advan- tages for England, employed all her influence in favour of peace and justice. He kept his eye steadily fixed on one result, that of Belgian independence, taking for his guide the desire to place the two countries of Holland and Belgium In such a position as would tend, when the generations which had raised their hands against each other had passed away, to draw their descendants together by connecting in- terests instead of tearing them apart by.conflicting passions. And, though Lord Palmerston's "little experimental Monarchy" was a never-failing subject of jest,the Foreign Secretary had the very great satisfaction of seeing his policy crowned with success. France certainly gained nothing by the transaction, while Europe had the advan- tage of possessing one more State which presented a favour- able example of Constitutional Government. The establishment of what has been termed the "Quad- ruple Treaty" is another result of Lord Palmerston' policy. This was a treaty of alliance negotiated by Lord Palmer- ston between England, France, Spain, and Portugal, and the object of it was the defence of the existing monarchies in the Peninsula against all attempts to displace them. Don Carlos laid claim to the Spanish throne, and Don Miguel to the Portngese. Their claims were really false, but, besides the weakness of their titles, they were obnoxious to the Foreign Secretary, on account of their antipathy to Consti- tutional Government. "The civilised world," exclaimed the indignant Statesman, "rings with execration upon , Miguel—this destroyer of Constitutional freedom, this breaker of solemn oaths, this faithless usurper, this enslaves' of his country, this trampler upon public law, this violater of private rights, and this attempter of the life of helpless and defenceless women." It is clear that the Foreign Secre- tary would etretch a point to thwart the designs of one of whom he held such a mean opinion. And he did stretch a point, to the indignation of the non-resistance party at home. But while the logic of debate belonged to Lord Aberdeen and his followers, Lord Palmerston had the still more strik- ing logic of success. True, he violated the principle of neutrality in sending British troops to the Peninsula, but the principle could never be absolute—the violation was necessary, and it proved to be beneficial. Perhaps the most brilliant of Palmerston's exploits as Foreign Secretary was an armed interference to prevent the dismemberment of the Turkish Empire. It is well known that Mehemet All, from being a mere vassal ef the Grand Seignior, had by his great ability raised himself as Pasha of Egypt into a position of real independence. Not content with the Pashalic of Egypt, he wished to add to it Syria, and with the assistance of his son Ibrahim proceeded te carry out his plan. Turkey was in a very critical position. It had practically lost Egypt, and was. now in danger of losing another province. Lord Palmerston determined to avert the catastrophe, and sought to draw the great Powers into a league for the preservation of the Ottoman Empire. France, under the guidance of M. Thieve, aimed at securing through its support of Mehemet All in his revolt against the Sultan a quasi control and patronage of Egypt. In the French Chambers it was openlv declared that the aim of France was " to establish a second-rate maritime power in the Mediterranean, whose fleet might unite with that of France for the purpose of serving as a counterpoise to that of England." Such a purpose was not likely to escape the penetrating eye of Lord Palmerston, and he set himself to defeat it on the broad ground that the Mistress of India could not permit France to be mistress, directly or indirectly, of the road to her Indian dominion!. A treaty was formed between England, Austria, and Turkey, by which a fleet was despatched to the scene of action. Acre was bombarded, and the fortress which had defied the first Napoleon was taken, and Mehemet All was finally driven from the country and compelled to give up his claim. The rapidity with which the exploit was conceived and executed, the daring of the attempt, and the magnitude of the result, gave a lustre to the reputation of Lord Palmerston, and rendered him at once the most popular Minister in England. "A timid Secretary of State in the position of Lord Palmer- ston," says Mr. Disraeli in one of hiebooks, "even with his advantages, might have faltered ; but the weapon was placed in the hands of one who did not shrink from its exercise, and the expulsion of the Egyptians from Turkey remains a great historic monument alike of diplomatic skill and ad- ministrative energy." , In 1841, on the fall of the Whig Cabinet, Lord Palmerston resigned the seals of the Foreign Office. But in those years which intervened between 1830 and 1841 he had kept up England as the Great State morally and materially of Europe. He had, on the whole, expressed her ideas, and had always maintained her intereB ts His language was clear and bold, and when he menaced action or thought action necessary he had ever been ready by his deeds to make good his language, yet in no instance had his free speech and ready courage led to those wars which timid poli- ticians fear, and bring about frequently by their apprehen- sions. In 1841, being out of office, and reviewing the Ses- sion, be claimed " to have handed over to the honourable gentlemen opposite the Foreign relations in a state as satis- factory, as secure, and as much calculated to inspire just confidence as they were ever at any former period in our history." div.head: BUDGET.
div.p: THE BUDGET.

Mr. GLADSTOM wl-n)-;as-r-e;eive-cl-with loud cheers, rose to make his financial statement, and at once plunged into th ) main facts +of the case. He said that the gross revenue of the year jest concluded is £84,041,000,as against an esti- mated revenue of £82,696,000. But this considerable in- crease, he added, was only apparent, and, analysing the different items, he showed that, while the estimated revenue from taxes was £69,436,000, its actual yield only rose to £69;814,000, so that thE great increase, amounting to £1,345,000, arose from such items as the Post Office and miscellaneous. As to the new taxes, he said the probate duties, estimated at £700,000, had only produced £640,000; the beer duty, estimated at £3,690,000, had only produced £3,485,000; while the drawback, conjectured at £950,000, had really cost £1,312,000. The total increase of the revenue over the preceding year was nearly two millions, of which the new taxes accounted for £1,019,000, so that the real in- crement of the revenue was only £969,000—a beginning, but only a beginning of recovery in the revenue. Mr. Gladstone next gave the House various particulars illus- trating the working of the conversion of malt duty to a beer tax, and especially showing how trade bad been liberated by the employment of new materials in brewing. He mentioned also venous small changes he intended to-make chiefly tor the benefit of private brewers, including an increase on the duty on spruce and a redaction of the duty on foreign beer to 135 61, Passing to the expenditure of the past year, he pointed out that, while the estimate was £83,840,000, the actual expenditure was £83,108,000, showing a reduction at £732,000, compared with the estimate, of £997,000, com- pared with the previous year, and, when compared with the "venue, showing a surplus of £933,000. Next he touched on the operations on the debt during the year, showing that It had been reduced by £5,325,000, and that the balances in the Exchequer had increased in thesametime by £2,650,000. But daring the year about a million of local loans had been repaid, so that, on the whole, the total reduction of debt had amounted to about £7,000,000. He reminded the House that in 1885 the short annuities would fall in, and was met with a very general cheer when he stated that he should regard it as an illegitimate use of those funds to apply them in reduction of taxation. He proposed, therefote,in a man- ner which he explained at length, to convert the short annuities into long annuities, terminating In 1906, by which a reduction of debt would be effected to the amount of £60,000,000, of which £20,000,000 would be taken from the Savings Bank and £40,000,000 from the Chancery Stock. Mr. Gladstone then went into a long digression on what he described as the movement of public wealth compared with population and expenditure. Taking three periods of time commencing with 1842, he showed that, while from 1842 to 1858 population bad increased * per cent per annum the re- venue lj per cent and the expenditure2iper cent, from 1857 to 1873 the augmentations were 1 per cent., 3 per cent., and 1* per cent: respectively, and from 1874 to 1877 1 per cent., 11 per cent., and 31. But in the last two years reaching down to March, 1880, while the population had increased by 1 per cent., the revenue had actually gone back one-half per cent, and the expenditure had increased by 2 1-6 per cent. In furper illustration of this he mentioned that the penny In the income-tax, which in 1842 produced £772,000, in 1858 £BlO,OOO, and in 1878 £1,990,000, in tbis last year, for the fife time in the history of the tax, had actually gone back and stood at £1,943.000. Passing to the finances of the present year he thus stated the estimated expenditure for 1881-2:--- Consolidated Fund Charges Army 16,509,000 , Home Charges for India 1,100,000 Navy 10,845,000 Grant in Aid to India Civil Services Customs and Inland Revenue 2,851,208 Post Office Telegraph Service Packet Service 707,767

Total expenditure (in round numbers) £84,705,000 This shows an increase over the actual expenditure of the preceding year of no less than £1,597,000., and in explaining this increase he dwelt on such itetfis as the census, the ordnance survey, and the necessary augmentation of the Irish constabulary, and showed that the exceptional charge for India and the Transvaal amounted to £1,800,000., and during the past year to £3,331,080. Proceeding to the other side of the account he stated the revenue for the year:— Customs £19,000,000 Excise Stamps Land-tax, ecc. Income-tax Post "Office Telegraphs Crown Lands Interest on advances . Miscellaneous Revenue

Total Revenue £85,990,000 This shows a surplus of revenue over expenditure of £1,285,000, which is, however' reduced by a charge to ex- tinguish the loan for barracks to £1,185,000. Coming to the question how this surplus is to be disposed Of, he said he regarded the sixth penny on the Income tax granted last year merely as a loan for a special purpose, and not an addi- tion to permanent taxation, and he proposed, therefore, to remit it. This would at a stroke convert the surplus into an actual deficit of £275,000. Before stating the mode in which this is to be made up, he canvassed various suggestions which had been made, concluding with regard to the tobacco duty that it is too early to form any judgment as to the success or failure of the change made by his predecessor, and stating his intention of proposing a gradual reduction of the duty oa silver plate at the rate of 3d per ounce annu- ally. The first proposal he had to make for increased revenue was an adjustment of the sur-tax on foreign spirits and rum. The process of distillation as practised with wines would .be applied to them, and a uniform hur-tax of 44: per gallon would be charged on the standard of strength. The net effect of this would be a gain of £lBO,OOO. The next subject he mentioned was the "Death duties," and at this there was a general cheer from the Ministerial benches, but he went on to say that he was not about to attempt any complete plan for dealing with them, though he hoped that the present Parliament would not expire without some ouch attempt being made to deal with them. Touching on the anomalies of the present system, he spoke strongly of the total exemption of property in mortmain, warmly condemned the differental rates imposed on personal property settled and unsettled, rand said with regard to the duties on real property, that they were so bound up with the laws regulat- ing its devolution and inheritance that it was impossible to I deal with them practically without going into the whole : question. Canvassing the scaloof consanguinity, heaaid he I• was not prepared at once to accept a uniform duty—One I effect Of which would be to increase the duty of lineals from j 1 to n per cent, but he was prepared to make some changes I which would be in the nature of an instalment andwould clear , the way by testing the disposition of the public. By the first I of these, where all parties concerned—the residuary legatees, the executors, and the In' and Revenue—are agreed, the whole , payment to the state .may be made at once in the shape of lan augmented 5 per cent. probate duty. Next he proposed Ito abolish the 1 per cent. legacy duty and to substitute a li per cert. probate duty, anethis, he said, while it would be I ' paid by the same parties, wonld get rid of the present cora- lplication. Among other changes, the duty will be charge- able on sums between £lOO and £l,OOO, at intervals of £5O, I and over £l,OOO, at interval of £100; the exemption from ' duty of legacies under £2O, is abolished, and where the parties can make:an affidavit that the estate does not exceed , £3OO in value, they may go before the nearest Revenue Officer, and diecharge all claims for probate and legacy duty by the payment of £2 Sc. The net financial gain of these changes is £467,000, but as the change will only come into operation on June'lst the gain this year is only £390.000. Adding this;to the £lBo,th enfroemtvbeertse the deficit of deficituteieist there is a total gain of 1570,00% w of £275,000 into a. surplus of £295,000. Mr. Gladstone,l after speaking a little over two hours, toncluded by remark- icg that this was, his 11th and in olosbly his last Budget.— In the desultory discussicn which followed a general ap- proval of the scheme was expressed by Sir S. Northcote, Mr. Hubbard, and Sir G. Goldnev. Mr. Dtdds regretted that the revision of the Probate Duties had not been carried further. Mr. Watney, Mr. Whitbread, and Mr. Storer made some observations on the Beer Tax. Mr. Andersons Mr. Maclver, Mr.'Ashnsead-Bartlett,, Mr. Biddel I, and Mr. Bux- ton spoke ; and Mr. H. Fowler, Mr. Lea, Mr. Illingworth, and Mr. Vifiggin complained of the excessive expenditure, and Mr. Gorst twitted the Alinisterialists with a violation of their economic pledges. ,Mr. Pease replied that the large military expenditure Was due to- the late Government, and eepecially to their foreign policyaud their treatmeit of.the Doers;' but this was denied by Sir- W. Barttelot and Mr. NI n, who charged Mr. Gladstone with the responsibility for the Transvaal war and the " peate with dishonour " by which it had been closed. The Budget resolutions were then agreed to. , . WARRINGTON POLICE CASES.
Monne.T.—Before Alderman Pieltme!e (mayor),. and
Councillorlaircough and Councillor.broifielci.

A LONG LTFF.—James Noon, charged with being drunk on Saturday, was fined 10s. and costs. This was- his 54th appearance. IN CHASE OF A PRISONZE.—JaHIea Spence!' was charged with stealing a cured ham, of the value of 6s. 6d., from the shop of John Gandy, grocer, Church-street, at 9-30 on Saturday night.—Prisoner was seen by prosecutor to take the ham from a hook in tie shop, but before he could get to him the priSoner had decamped. After a long chase be was captured by a police officer, but the ham could not be found. A search was subsequently made in a pigeon cote of the de. fendant's, and the ham discovered concealed in a corner, with a piece cut out.—Prisoner was committed to prison for one month. A DESERTER.—Edward Brown was charged with being a deserter from the 4th Royal Lancashire Militia.—Prisoner pleaded guilty, and said it was five years since he deserted. —He was fined 40s. and costs, or, in default, one month.— P.C. Taylor, who had captured the man, applied for the usual reward, and he was recommended to be paid 11. OFFENCE AGAINST THE FacTorts Aer.—Thounas Hunt, a fustian cutter, was charged with having, on the 16th March, unlawfully employed Ann Hines and May y Ann Lee for more than seven days without having obtained cer- tificates of fitness as required by the Factory and Workshops Act.—Captain Meade-King, inspector of factories, said that on the 24th February be went to the defendant's shop and found one child had been employed six, and another twelve months without the requisite certificate having been ob- tained. On visiting the shop again on the 16th March, having then given defendant three weeks to put the matter straight, he found the same persons still employed without certificates.—As Captain Meade-King did not press the charge, the Bench fined defendant ss. and costs in each case. .

MR. HARAISTON'S CIRCUS.—Mr. Moore applied on behalf of Mr. Harmston for permission to perform the play of "Dick Turpin "at his circus in Sankey-street. —The Clerk: We have had a prisoner here this morning named Jack Shepherd. (Laughter.)—Mr. Moore :We shall have Robin Hood next. (Laughter.) Mr. Moore said the usual time required before such an application could be granted was 14 days, but Mr. Harmstoa would like it, if possible, in a week.—The Mayor : I suppose it is an ordinary applica- tion ?—Mr. Moore: It is merely a matter of form. The application was granted DRUNKEN CARTERS.—Joseph Burrows, a carter, was charged with being drunk in charge of a horse and cart, in Bridge-street, on the 25th March. Defendant pleaded guilty, and he was fined Sc., including costs.—John Kelly was mulcted in a similar stun for a like offence, committed on the 28th Marsh. THE MARKET INSPECTOR AND HIS BUTIII3.—JSMeS Bow- cock, a respectably dressed man was charged with being drunk and disorderly in the. market, ret, on the fith March. P.C. Chantler proved the case.—Mr. Hunt Why was not the case reported before this?—P.C. Chantler said Mr. Place stated to him that offences committed in the market had to be reported to the Market Committee.—The Mayor: Was it reported to the committee? Yes, and they ordered the case to be proceeded with.—Mr. Hunt remarked that Mr. Place was a sworn constable, and it would be much better if the cases were proceeded against at the time instead of coming up now.—The Mayor said he would write and bring the neittter before the notice of the committee.—Defendant was fined sa. and costs. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASIS.—John Clare was summated for neglecting to send his son John Thomas regularly to school. Mr. Riley said this was the third time defendant had been before the court, and the boy had made very few attendances during the past year. Defendant was fined ss. —A similar charge MS preferred against Henry Lawton. Mr. Riley said the child had only made 22 attendances out of a possible 110. She could not read or write, and was alto- gether in a very lost condition. A fine of 55. was imposed. —John Clifton was summoned for not sending his son to school regularly. Mr. Riley said the, boy played truant for weeks together, and had not been to the school for the last five months. Defendant pie vied ignorance. The boy had always pretended to do his lessons at night. He gave him his school money every week. The father stating that he could do no good with the boy and being willing that he should flogged, the Bench ordered him twelve strokes. —John Lawless was summoned for not sending a girl under his charge to school. Mr. Riley observed that the Board of Guardians had paid the fees since 1879, and she bad not attended one fifth of ber time. She could neither read nor write, and she was in such a wretched condition that the master of one school had been obliged to get rid of ter. Mr. Crossfield considered defendant to blame, and he was fined 55.--James Williams was summoned for not sending his daughter regularly to school. Defendant's wife appeared, and Mr. Riley said he wished defendant had appeared as he used his wife shamefully. The woman said her husband was not at home. Mr. Hunt: Have the bailiffs taken him? Witness: Yes, to Walton. Mr. Crosfield : Does he work for us? , Witness: He has not done any for the last five weeks.—Mr. Crosfield.: It is a shameful thing and if that child is not sent to school, he shall work for us no more. The case was ad- journed for two months to give the parents another oppor- tunity of sending the child to school. A fine of Sc. was im- posed on William Cunningham and John Towey, for similar offences. For net sending his children Mary, and Thomas to school, Owen O'Donnell was fined Sc. in each case.—Ann Muegrove, widow, was summoned for not sending her son William regular to school] y. Mr. Riley said this case bad been often before the Bench, but the attendance at school was still very bad. Defendant was for a long time assisted by the Board of Guardians and many ladies in the town, but she kept her children in a a veil, ragged and dirty condition. The Mayor said it seemed defendant worked as much as she could, and eked the rest out by begging from charitable people keeping her children in wretchedness and misery. The children ought to go to the Workhouse where they could be properly attended to. Mr. Crosfield said the best thing that could be done for the lad was to send him to an industrial school. Defendant, however, would not consent to such a course, and an order as made for the attendance of the boy at King-street school. Tau Cass or zuu Ray. S. F. GREEN.—In the Queen's Bench Division, on Wednesday, the ease of the Rev. Sidney Fairborne Green, rector of Miles Platting, was before Justices Grove and Lindley. Mr. Charles, Q.C., with whom were Mr. Poland and Dr. Phillimore, moved for a writ of habeas corpua to fissile to the keeper of Her Majesty's prison at Lancaster Castle to bring up the Rev. Sidney Fairborne Green to this court with a view to his discharge from custody. He moved upon an affidavit of Mr. Green, who stated that on the LOth March, 1881, he was arrested and conveyed•to the gaol at Lancaster Castle, ivhere he was still detained in custody, and he submitted to their lordships that Mr. Green should be discharged from custody upon three grounds—first, that Lord Penzancn had no jurisdiction to summon Mr. Green to appear before him at Westminster, where the cause was heard and determined in respect of which Mr. Green bad now been detained for con- tempt, and that Lord Penzance had no power to issue his significavit from Westminster; secondly, that the whole of the proceedings subsequent to the significavit were void, because the writ against Mr. Green of de contumo,cia cavienda could not be issued by the Vice-Chancellor of the County Palatine of Lancaster, but only by the High Court of Justice; and thirdly, that the same official had no juris- diction to issue his writ of attachment when sitting in his room in Litte.A.gn's Inn.—Their lordships having heard argu- ments of a technical character based tpon those points, refused to grant a Writ upon any of ,the grounds set forward.

The Army Discipline and Regulation Bill was read a second time. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNBSDAY. Raw WRIT.—A new writ was ordered to be issued for Sunderland to fill the vacancy caused by Sir H. M. Have- lock-Allen accepting a military command. TEE IRISH LAND BILL.—Mr. Smyth withdrew his Irish Land Bill, in the confident hope, he explained, that the measure which the Premier was about to introduce would give security to Ireland and satisfy all just expectations without injury to any class. TER LUNACY LAW ASSIMILATION BILL.-MT. Litton moved the second reading of the Lunacy Law Assimilation (Ireland) Bill. He explained that the object of the bill naa to give facilities for the enlarging of the asylums, to adbpt the English syqtem with respect to pauper lunatics, and the Scotch boardinpout system, and, what was most important of all, to provide for efficient inspsetion. In the course of the debate, the Solicitor-General for Ireland said the Govern- ment would offer no opposition to the second reading of the bill, but it would require very considerable amendment in committee to make it workable. The bill was read a second time, the committee being fixed for the Ist of June.

COPYHOLD ENFEAMUISEMENT BILL.—On the motion of Mr. Waugh, the Copyhold Enfranchisement Bill was read a second time. The object of the bill is to provide for the gradual compulsory conversion of copyhold into freehold tenure, with the object of cheapening transfers and clearing the way for a registration of titles. TEE LAND BILL: MR. GLADSTONE'S REMEDIES FOR lamat DISCONTENT.—Mr. GLADEroNE was loudly cheered on rising to move for leave to introduce the Irish Land Bill. The right hon. gentleman said the subject was the most difficult and complex he had ever had to deal with. He denied that the existing land laws of Ireland could truly be described as "iniquitous," and said that one of the diffi- culties in the way of a fair settlement of the question had been the promulgation of schemes of "public plunder." Nor could it be said that the general body of Irish landlords had been guilty of misconduct, but there were landlords who had brought dishonour on their cites by the arbitrary raising of rents and by harsh and cruel evictions. He admitted that Serious defects in the Act of 1870 had been developed. The bill new propased had been framed with a view to ensuring the due exercise of the landlord's rights so as not to destroy fair competition, while there was also a recognition of the right of the tenant to assign his interest. The cardinal institution ef the measure was the establishment of a court that would take cognisance of rent. It was proposed thaeltecess to the Court should he perfectly free—optional and not compulsory. The judicially-fixed rent should endure for 15 years without change, and during that time there should be no eviction except for breach of covenant er non-payment of rent. At the close of the 15 years the landlord might with the appro- val of the Court and under fixed conditions resume posses- sion. The bill gave tile landlord a right of pre-emption if the tenant wished to sell his right. As to tenancies held by these who had no wish to call in the power of the Court, the tenant would be vested with the right of assign- ment, and the landlord with that of applying or a termination of the tenancy on reasonable grounds. Tenants might remain under the Ulster custom as now, but have the protection of the bill for controlling augmentations of rents. If the tenant wished he would be at liberty to pass from the Ulster custom and go under the provisions of the bill. The bill saught to amend the law as to compensation for improvements. It was proposed that any lease to be exempted from the bill must be a judicial lease. Fixed tenancies might be constituted by the Court when the landlord and tenant were agreed. There was no power to contract out of the measure except where the valuation amounted to £l5O. Provision was made for the establishment of a land com- misson to deal with cases where public advances might be necessary. The Commissioners would have power to assist tenants to purchase, and also power to purchase estates from willing landlords for re-sale to the tenants.. Where three-fourths of a tenantry in number and value wished to purchase the Commissioners might advance three- fourths of the money, but the tenants would not be allowed to sub-let or sub-divide their holdings while they remained under charge. Advances might also be granted to promote emigration, in the first pla.ce to colonial Governments, and in the next place to companies. The Premier, in conclusion, pointed to the improvement that had taken place in the con- dition of the Irish people in late years, and expressed a con- fident hope that. the measure he wee introducing would confer further advantages upon the country.—Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE abstained from discussing the principles ef the measure.—ln a conversatiok which followed, Mr. SEAw 'bespoke a candid consideration for the bill on the part of his countrymen.—Mr. PARNELL criticised the provision as to emiaration, but reserved his judgment on the main provisions of the bill. _ -

WARGRATE-RO•D AND • SEWEIIA.GE SCHEME. The CHAIRMAN, referring to tho sewering of Wargrave- road, said there seemed to be a difficulty as to how to deal with it. Birley, Winstanley, Emmett, and Pardey, was appointed to wait upon the railway company ia reference to the matter.

TAR HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. Dr. Wevms, the medical officer, read his quarterly report. There were registered—Births, males 51, females 43, total 94; deaths, males 28, females 32, total 60. The excess of births over deaths was—males 23, females, 11, total 34. The birth rate was 32.10, and the death rate 2049, per 1,000 of the estimated population to the first of April, but undoubt- edly a corrected estimate would show the rate to be higher-. Scarlet fever: under five years of age 10, five yearrand up- wards 4; whooping cough, 4,1; fever (classihed as gastric), 1, —; erysipelas, —, 1; puerperal fever, —, 6 ; pthysis, 3; pulmonary inflammation, 3,4; heart diseases, —, 5' injuries, —, 1 ; other diseases, 11, 6; total 29,31. Thus it will be seen that the wide-spread sicknes and the high rate of mortality that pertained in the last quarter of 1880 has been maintained in this quarter. Scarlet fever caused 14 deaths-2 33 per cent, of the total deaths-10 of children under five years, and the remaining four between that age, and eight years. Two common causes of the spread of the disease and of the deaths, exist in the insufficient isolation of the sick and the early exposure of patients apparently recoyeriug, but whose expected convalesence is thus arreqted quite suddenly, and their condition converted always into one of danger, terminating, in many cases, in death. Six out of the ten children under Rye years of age who died succumbed, not in the early stage of the fever, but from the sequels of the disease, such as "post," scarlatinal, dropsy, disease of the lungs, the. So much misapprehension un- happily prevails on this subject that I may be permitted in the public interest to impart some information to those whom it most nearly concerns. In a certain proportion of cases in scarlet fever the elevation of the temperature reaches its height about the fourth day of the disease and becomes normal about the seventh. But in these cases, and often in the mildest ef them, this fever is but the first stage of the disease which has to develops some of Its more important features. There is a second stage of 'the disease which occurs usually seine-time within 14 days of the termination of the first or febrile stage, and consist most frequently of affections of the kidney, the lymphatic glands and mucuous, and Berns membranes, any of which may have I either immediately fatal results or lay the foundation of permanent disease of the kidney, the heart, or the brain. It is on account of the changes which take place in this second stage of the disease that physicians recommend that scarlet fever patients should keep their beds, or at least their rooms, until this period shall have passed, because injudicious ex- posure, such for instance as to the recent inclement weather, might not only change into permanent disease, morbid pro- cesses which are proceeding naturally to health, but be immediately fatal by the supervention of dropsy in every part of the body, the most dangerous form of croup, or by acute rheumatism, complicated with disease of ttle heart or lungs. And these possibilities, it is to be noted, apply in a special degree to the cases:in which the first or febrile stage is mild, and where parents are naturally inclined to think that there is little need for particular care. The first stage, which ends about the seventh day, is to be followed by the second stage which ends in the milder cases towards the termination of the third or forth week. In the feregoing remarks it has been jny object to point out the grave risks which the patient himself would incur by exposure even in mild cases, or early—so early as the eighth day. We have only to add that there is no ground whatever for the assumption that the infectious material of scarlet fever is confined to the skin and its cuticle. Leaving out of account discharges from the throat and lungs and the affection of the bowels there is a very frequent, if nct indeed invariable and abundant, morbid process going on in the internal structure of the kidney, which takes place frem the third or fourth week, and this there is no reason to believe to be less infectious than the process of the peeling of the skin. The arrangement recently made by the Commissioners with the Warrington Corpora- tion for the reception into their special hospital of any cases of infectious diseases that may be sent there should enable us in many cases to effect that isolation which is so essentially necessary, and thereby to limit the foci of infec- tion. The report concluded by remarking that six deaths from puerperal fever, ten per cent, of the whole, was as deplorable as extraordinary, and were clearly traceable to the ' preventible epidemic. Be had made careful inquiry. of the medical men who certified these cases, and only in two were the patients under medical "and special care from the first. These patients had five different nurses (midwives). One patient-bad nursed her two children; one of them died of scarlet fever, and two women died in the Same street. A poor woman, just about from her own confinement, nursed a neighbour in hrs. The latter contracted fever and died; her friend caught the diseasa from her, and paid the penalty ' of her devotion by her life. The utmost care was impera- tively necessary by every midwife and nurse who had had communication, personally or otherwise, between infected cases or :.houses; and culpable negligence was subject to severe.punishment if proved. O'Comeon moved the adjournment of the House in order to call attention to the fatal riots in Ireland and the adminis- tration of the Coercion Act.—After a reply by Mr. Forster, Mr. JUSTIN DPC.airrav accused the Govern- ment of having fomented the agitation in Ire- land and then "turned round, upon the Irish members when it suited their purpose."—Mr. Guagrrown thought that if the Irish representatives had any serious charges to bring against the Government they ought to be brought forward in another form than under cover of a motion for the adjournment of the House. The Compensation Bill had been referred to, but the Govern- ment got very little assistance from the Irish members in regard to that bill. It was untrue that the Government had brought in that measure for the purpose Of fomenting agita- tion between the Land Leaguers and tenants. As to the attitude of the Government and the language they had used, he could may for himself that he • had exercised great self- repression in dealing with the Irish question, and in keeping hie language within the bounds to which he had confined it, for he held that great mischief might be done by a minister who unduly mixed his own private feelings and delires with the grave questions pending between England and Ireland. The fact was that the Go fernment had allowed themselves to be torn from the purposes they had cherished when they first took office in order that they might apply the needed remedies to the state of things existing in Ireland, and in the work they had already spent the greater part of the session. They were now about to bring in a measure deal- ing with the land question, and he could say that never in his knowledge had any Government exercised greater care or bestowed more anxious labour on the consideration of any proposal they had put before Parliament, with the view of applying the searching remedy which they believed both justice and policy demanded.-11r.
