div.head: ST. HELENS PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: ST. HELENS PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.

DINNER TO THE SPEAKER. As an appropriate wind-up to the first session of this society, the members determined to give a dinner in honour of the Speaker (Dr. McNicol.) Thursday evening was the time fixed for the event, and a large company assembled in the large room of the Fleece Inn, where a most excellent repast was served up by Mrs. Taylor and her assistants in a manner that added to the repute of the well-known hostelry. Dr. McNicol occupied the post of honour, and was supported by, among other gentlemen, His Worship the Mayor, Major Ogle, Mr. H. L. Riley, Mr. Massey, ac. The CHAIRMAN proposed, in very felicitous terms, "The Queen." and "The Prince and Princess of Wales and the rest of the Royal family," and both toasts were received with musical honours. Mr. W. .1. MARROW proposed the "Army, navy, and reserve forces," whose discipline and courage he spoke of in the highest terms of praise, and concluded amid applause by coupling with the toast the name of Major Ogle. "Army and navy duet," by Mr.,Cr. Barton and Mr. Edwd. Fidler. Major OGLE, in responding, said he had often experienced a great degree of pleasure in responding for the defenders of our country, but he bad never felt so much pleasure as he did at that moment. Those assembled there that night had been for some months past two enemies pitched against each other, but now they were all there gathered together in a friendly manner. (Hear, hear.) He could not make out whether the toast was best re.ceived by the Ministerial party or by the Opposition. (Laughter.) But he thanked them for the hearty manner in which they had received the toast. The army was in a state of reorganisation, and they scarcely knew what it was or what it would to. Some time since the long service period was done away with, and six years under colours and six years in the reserve forces was substituted. The short service period brought a great many young men into the ranks, but it was felt that it was too short a time to be under colours. A young fellow who entered at 18 years of age, and was six years under colours, was only 24 when he left. They knew that a man 20 years of age was capable of any duty at home, bat campaign life abroad was very trying upon the constitutions of young men. By the proposed reorganisation he understood it was , intended that the reserve forces should be brought into closer amalgamation with the army than before. In a short time the numbering of regiments would be dene away with. They would be known by names, such at the City of Dublin, Warwickshire, Lancashire. A great many would bear different names in Lancashire, for instance, Liverpool, Man- chester, dx. In each case two line regiments would he ' formed into one battalion, and two militia regiments would be attached to them, thus making four regiments into one battalion. It was expected that the volunteers would be joined to them; and in time the volunteer regiments would be called upon to give men to the line to go out and fight the , country's battles. (Hear, hear.) If volunteers would go ' out they would be of the greatest advantage to the line. ' They knew from experience in St. Helens what admirable shooting qualities there were among the volunteers. (Hear, ' hear.) Having expressed his opinion that crack shots in an engagement would be worth any amount of money, be paid a high compliment to the St. Helens volunteers for their efficiency. ( Applause.) Mr. J. MASSEY (the Premier), who was received with ap- plauee, rose to move the next toast. He said he did not know whether he should describe it as a pleasing duty that the toast of the evening should have fallen into his hands. , It would have pleased him far better if the toast had fallen , into other hands. He never liked to praise personal friends in their presence,but when that was done he w ished it to be done In an efficient way. He did not know whether they had a pre- cedent in imperial proceedings for giving A banquet to the Speaker. If not, he thought the present Ministry might take a hint from them. (Hear, bear, and cheers.) The society, over which the Speaker presided so ably, had been in exis- tence something like four months. By that society, when , Loth parties met, the Speaker was unanimously selected to preside over its deliberations. (Hear, bear.) That was a compliment to him, and a testimony to his ability. All I. political parties, including the Horne Rulers and the Fourth I Party—(laughter.)—were all agreed that he was the most", fitted of the St. Helens gentlemen to preside over them. I (Hear, hear.) He thought that that was the feeling that night,—(hear, hearl,—and it was an honour that would con- , vince the Speaker that be had discharged his duties to their. satisfaction. He thought that that bancoet was a very k3ppy idea, but he did net know by whom it was originated. ; ilt served the purpose of paying a compliment to the Speaker, I and of uniting both political parties in a social gathering. (Hear, hear.) It would tend to cement personal friendahip and to keep the society afloat until next session. During the , time the Speaker had acted as president, he had seen one; Ministry everthrown, and he had witnessed another Ministry I defeated, that had not thought fit to resign. (Laughter.) I The Speaker had acted throughout the session with maim- ; tiality, and his rulings had given the utmost satisfaction. I When they remembered that the Speaker was a great political partisan—and he said it with the greatest deference—and that they might expect him to ; have a leaning to his own party, he (Mr. Massey) must say ' that he had given the Conservatives fair play and had ruled impartially. (Hear, hear.) If they had another session— "and he hoped they would—he trusted that Dr. McNicol would continue to be their speaker, and to discharge the duties as he bad done in the past. (Hear, hear.) A gentle- man of his position and ability was of great help to the , society, and if it were net for gentlemen like him societies of that description might go to the dogs, and the young men of St. Helens be deprived of something that tended to the development of their minds. (Hear, hear.) Dr. McNicol discharged a duty te the town when he filled the chair in the way he did. He had merely spoken of Dr. McNicol as the Speaker; iffhe were to speak of Lim as a friend—and he was sure he was a friend of all of them— he was afraid he !should speak too long. Dr. McNicol had been foremost in .aiding every movement for the advancement of the young !'inen of the town. (Hear, hear.) That was acknowledged thy all; and it was that feeling which prompted them to ask him to become the Speaker of the Society. He trusted that the Speaker would long continue to have the good opinion of the people, and that he would litre long and be secured every happiness. (Applause.) The West was enthusiastically, drunk, and Mr. Barton's glee party sang an amusing catch entitled "The Speaker." Dr. Meehan (the Speaker) was greeted with applause on rising to respond. He thanked them all for the cordial Manner in which they bad received the toast, and Mr. Massey for the kindly sentiments and compliments in which he had proposed it. From the first, though that movement did not originate with him, he threw himself into it, as he could conceive of no better thing after the toils of a week than to engage in debates of a political character. A man required a variety of occupations, and if he could ride a hobby at nights after his day's work, he would live all the longer for it. Nothing could be hatter than to meet at the end of a week to have a political tournament, horse to horse, and try to unhorse one onother. The meetings of the society bad been conducted very courteously. Sometimes there had been considerable spirit shown, but they all bad their peculiar temperaments. He could not accept the satire their musical friends had represented. They had not been so disorderly, but had on the whole kept very good order. rWhilat they had been courteous to one another, they had been deferential to the chair. His election to the Speaker's chair gave him as much satisfaction as anything that had been done during the 32 years he had been in St. Helens. (APPlause.) The proposal came from the Conservative party, to which he did not belong, and when he knew that his appointment was by a unanimous vote he could not find words to say how glad he was. (Hear, hear.) Some might think it no honour to be elected to the office of Speaker over a society of a number of youug men. But he did. (Hear, hear.) A gentleman said to him that day, "Why, McNicol, you ought to feel as much honoured as if they had made You Mayor." (Applause.) If the aldermen and councillors ' had uaade him Mayor—which they never would do—he could not have been so well pleased as be was when he was unanimously elected to occupy the chair. It was a great conpliment to him. It was saying that he had the sense and ability to fill the office, and that he could be trusted to act impartially. (Hear, hear.) He had said that variety WWI life to an individual A political body wanted activity, and it must not be permitted to become stagnant. Political Parties were the very life of the nation. (Hear, hear.) He thanked them veryanuch for the high honour they had paid him, and also.for that banquet that they had been pleased to give to him, as well as for the cordial manner in which his health had been received. Mr. Hone/max proposed "The Chairman of Committees and officers of the house," and, in the absence of the Chair- , man of Committees, coupled with the toast the name of Mr. Knighton, clerk of the heuse. Glee--" Come, boys, drink." Mr. Keneurrox, in responding, said that the society slum- bered 400 members, and that they had a balance in the bank of £25 to begin the next session with.
Mr. Robinson, Mr. Muir, and Mr. Wilson, party whips, also responded.

Mr. H. L. ar-RY (Leader of the Opposition) proposed "The Ministry," without which, he said, the society mild not exist. Though some people were inclined to make fun of their mimic parliament and mimic political speeches, he contended that the society was an excellent educational institution, and would fit those who did not rise to the im- perial legislature to become administrators in local govern- ments. The ministry, which was now holding a somewhat uncertain tenure of office, he believed, with all sincerity, possessed those requisites which every statesman should possess, namely, character, capacity, and courage. In felicitious terms he described how the courage of the minis- try had been exemplified by their deelaratioa when they took office to bring forward a large number of sweeping measures; and he concluded a hurnourous speech by appeal. log to the assembly to join him in drinking to the health of the gentlemen who formed the ministry of their house. (Applause.) The toast was drunk with enthusiasm, and afterwards the glee party sang " Life's a bumper." Mr. DEE (Chancellor of the Exchequer) briefly acknow- ledged the compliment. Mr. M. HAMMILL (Secretary for Foreign Affairs) proposed "The Opposition," and remarked that that evening's pro- ceedings was an evidence that they did not permit political bias to interfere with their personal friendships or social gatherings. If a Ministry was essential an Opposition was indispensable; and the Opposition, under Mr. Riley had been vigorous, perfectly fair, and generous. (Hear, hear.) Glee, " Comrades in arms."

THE OFFICE OF OVERSEER. A letter was read from the Clerk to the Guardians of the Salford Union, forwarding copy of memorial to the Local Government Board, asking for the abolishment of the office of overseer of the poor. He asked for the co-operation of the PrescOt Guardians in the matter.
Mr. P. Lox Grow : Refer it to the General Putposes Com- mittee.
Mr. FIDLER : I should think they will object to that. Mr. TIRER : I think the sooner they are abolished the better.
VOTE OF THANXS.

The Req. T. CILLMBERS proposed a vrte of thanks to the Chairman for his services during the past year. He could say from his heart—and no doubt it would be the feeling of his brother Guardians—that if he had erred at all it had been on the side of kindness. The Chairman had guided them with a silken thread. Mr. ROWE seconded the motion, which was carried with acclamation.

The CHAIRMAN said be was pleased at their expressions of kindness. If he were returned again, he hoped his con- duct would at all times meet with their approval. There was one failing which he had, and that was making use of language which he had no right to make use of. That was, perhaps, in consequence of being mixed up with so many matters, and the company he was prone to keep at times. (Loud laughter.)

div.head: PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD.
The last meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday at the offices, Derby-street, Mr. Wycherley presiding.
A FOOTPATH FOR &WELL-STREET,

The minutes of the General Purposes Committee showed that the Surveyor had invited the attendance of the owners of property abutting upon Aspinall-street, and all had agreed to the terms proposed by the Surveyor except Mr. Stephen Menzies, ;I ho had not replied to the circular or attended. The question was to consider the formation of a footpath along the street, and the clerk was directed to write to Mr. Menzies and ask him if he would contribute his quota of the expenses.—The Surveyor reported that the contractor for the St. Helene Dieu ict Tramways Company had seen him, and they had arranged the terms upon which the roads should be broken up for the purpose of laying the rails within the district of the Board. The contractor had written to say that he was agreeable to bear the expense of a man to protect the footpath and direct the traffic; also to pay reasonable expenses of making good any damage caused in the carrying out of the work,ind not open more than the- length of road mentioned in the Act of Parliament. The minutes were confirmed.
NEXT YEAR'S ESTIMATE.

The minutes of the Finance Committee contained the estiruqte of the Surveyor for the year ending March 25th, 1882 :—Total estimate, .£1,731 ; rateable value of the dis- trict, £14,147 155.; showing that a rate of 3s. 10d. was necessary to maks up the sum required. The minutes were confirmed, and it was agreed to lay the rate.

MORTALITY FOR TRH MONTE. The REGISTRAR'S return for the month showed 12 births In Prescot, and 2 in Eccleston, compared with 19 in Prescot and 5 in Eccleston, in the corresponding month last year. There had been in the same priod 16 deaths in Prescot, and 1 in Eccleston,.as against 12 in Prescot, and none in Eccleston in the corresponding mouth Ilst year. The rate of mortality per thousand is 34.04, compare.; with 24 04 in corresponding period last year.

TEE PRESSURE IN THE WATER MAINS. A letter was read from the Deputy Water Engineer of Liverpool in reply to a letter which the Board had written, complaining of a want of pressure in the water mains at Prescot, that the state of matters which gave rise to these complaints was mainly due to the late frost—in the first instance by consumers leaving the taps open to prevent the freezing of the water in the pipes, and thereafter by leakage from pipes fractured by the frost; also by a partial obstruction of the outlet where the water for Prescot was screened. This obstruction was cleared last Saturday.

M. SPENCELY ON THE CONDITION OF THE BOARD'S AFFAIRS. A letter was read from Mr. Spencely stating he regretted being unable to be „present at that the last meeting of the Board as at present constituted. • Much good work had been done during the past year and great improvement made in the sanitary state of the town, and in the roads and streets ;. and while this bad been done without any increase of the burden of the ratepayers, it had been so done that it would effect a reduction in future ex- penses. He adverted upon the satisfamory condition of the finances, which be thought the ratepayers would under- stand.

VOTES OF THANES. Mr. WYCIIERLEY proposed a vote of thanks to the Chair- man, to Mr. Cross (the clerk), and Mr. Goldsworth (the surveyor) for their services daring the year, and paid a compliment to their abilities.
Mr. Cross and Mr. GolciswOrth replied, and thanked them for their expression of kindly feeling, the latter remarking • that their chairman had done a great deal of work outside the Board.
IsTISLNCES.
The NUIS/tNCE INSPECTOR reported several nuliances which existed, and the clerk was instructed to write the owners of the property calling their attention to the matter.

'DEFECTIVE DELIVERY OF VOTING PAPERS. Mr. Wviancrircv said the manner in which the voting papers bad been delivered was the cause of a great deal of complaint and illfeeling in the town. Year after year large numbers of ratepayers did not receive voting papers. He understood there were a large number in Sewell-street. This ought to be done as efficiently as the taking of the census.
Mr. MAWDSLEY corroborated Mr. Wycberley's statement, and added there were some informal voting papers, and the question was who was to blame.

a Mr. GALLOWAY said a g-re7t-cieal of fault lay in the police- men, as the non-delivery did not occur indiscriminately, but in particuLar places. Mr. Cuoss said the papers were delivered according to the rate book, and the owners having to pay rates for small houses the .necessary care was net exercised in keeping the occupier's names down.

Finn AT S. Ileteim.—At 1.30 p.m. on Wednesday, an alarm was received of an outbreak of fire at Mr. J. Mort's hay and straw shed, Kirkland-street. The firemen, under Superintendent Birchall, were soon on the spot with a reel, and with a good supply of water from the corporation mains the fire was soon extinguished: A cab was removed slightly damaged from the burning shed. Superintendent Johnston and Inspector Wood with a small body of police were also in attendance. The cause of the fire is unknown, but the damage, amounting to £25, is covered by insurance in the London and Lancashire Fire Office. VE.STAY JARETING AT RAINSILL. —The annual meet- ing of the ratepayers of the township of Rainhill was held cn Friday, at Mr. Peter Fosr's, Victoria Hotel, Rainhill, Mr. Edward Johnson Brown presided, and there were a large attendance. The retiring overseers this year were Messrs. J. liubberstey and W. Lowe. Tha following gentiQmen were nominated to fill the vacancies —Messrs. J. Hubberstey, W. Lowe, John Hatton, James Forshavr, J. H. Gregory, and T. Naylor. The • sanitary accounts (special) showed a balance in hand of £132 14s. Si.; received from rate made 22nd November, 1879, £ll2 is. 10d.; ditto from rate made, 17th November, 1880, £156 7s. bd. The expenditure was as follows ;—Faid treasurer of Sanitary Authority, £3SS; other expenses, £l6 45. Bd.; leaving a balance due to overseers of 11d. Lighting accounts :—Receipts from rates, tic., £B6 15s. 6d. • expendi- ditare, 1130 Os. 11d.; balance due to overseers £43 Sc. sd. On the motion of Mr. W. H. Wheeler, seconded by Mr. J. B. Thompson, a hearty vote of thankg was passed to the overseers for the excellent manner hr which they had discharged the duties of their office during the past year. Mr. Matthew Lowe, the retiring waywarden, submitted his accounts, from which it stiemed that the cost of maintenance of the roads in the township had been £686 18s.; amount to be repaid by the county, £ll4 3s. Thi" • length of highway in the townehip was 7 miles 6 furlongs 37 yarde ; length of county roads, 2 miles 4 furlongs; total, 10 Miles 2 furlongs 37 yards. On the motion of Mr. Win. Lowe, seconded by Mr. Thomas Naylor, Mr. M. Lowe was unanimously re-appointed waywardea for the,eesuing year. The meeting elotredmith a vote of thanks to the Ch air n. r , ,

NOW COMPILING KELLY'S DIRECTORY OF LANCASHIRE with Maps engraved for the Work. Price to Subscribers, 405.; Non-Subscribers, 500. The Pub- lishers, in submitting the Prospectus of the Fourth Edition of the Directory of this County, respectfully hope for a con- tinuance of the patronage of their former Subscribers. The work will contain a topographical acoount of each Parish, Tillage, Hamlet, and Township, with its distance trans London and other objet towns, its position in the division of the County, Hundred and Union, and County Court District, and also the Diocese, Archdeaconry and Rural Deanery; Des- cription of the Churches, with the Value of the Living, and the names of the Patron ani Incumbent the shief landowners; the Acreage, notice of Soil and Crops, Local Chariti-s. and des- cription of the Principal Seats. In the towns are also given a short historical account, paiticulars of the Local Government; an Architectural Description of the Churches and other Public Buildings, Chapels of different Denominations; Public Schools, a full account of the Principal Manufacturies of which each *town is the seat; the Markets, Fairs, and Faces; Agricultural and Scientific Societies and Meetings, to.; Objects of Natural Curiosity and Antiquities; Hospitals, EAlmshouses and Charities. The Directory of each town comprises Lilts at the Resident Nobility, Clergy, and Gentry, and also a list of all engaged in Professional and Mercantile Pursuits. in Alphabetical Order. Information relating to Law and Public Offices, Churches and Chapels, the arrival and departure of the Mails and Coaches, Posting Houses, Commercial Inns, together with psrticulars respecting Conveyance by Railway, Vtater or Land Carriers. will also be included. Immediately following will be given an Alphabetical Arrangement of Names of the Nobility. Clergy, and Gentry, and a General Classification of Trades, which will exhibit all the Persons engaged in any Trade throughout the County. The Proprietors respectfully request the favour of .the gentlemen in their employ being personally seen on their applying for infor- mation, and that the precise spelling of the Name, 4c., may be given to them. I Mr. Gladstone leaves as it stands for another year; remarking that the lower price of the raw material for tobacco just now enables dealers and consumers to buy tobacco nearly as cheap as if the duty had not been raised. After the above reductions and readjust- ments, the estimated revenue for this year will be roundly £85,000,000, and the estimated expenditure £84,705,000 ; an estimated surplus of £300,000 balancing the account. We can never reckon befero hand to have a million what the taxes will yield—so much depends upon trade, the seasoas and crops, and other eventualities, so it is necessary to leave a small margin: But if this Government of peace can succeed in preserving peace in all quarters throughout the year, we may look forward at the end of the financial year to a financial surplus of Gladstonian proportions, with the further reductions of our taxes such a sur- plus will warrant. 1.

Notwithstanding the spread of education ,the pre- sent age is still very credulous, or two such characters as the "Dr; and Mrs. Lilly," who were apprehended at Wigan, and charged at Bristol this week with contravening the Medical Act, would not be able so successfully to carry on their trade of gulling and deceiving foolish people by their pretensions to the art of healing. It is said that an American quack once settled in a certain town where he at- tained such popularity that he soon brought the regular doctors to the verge of ruin. One day a man was taken to him suffering from an accident which rendered amputation of the leg necessary. To the astonishment of the faculty the quack performed the operation with surgeon-like Skill, causing one of them to ask him how it was that he being merely a quack was able to show such professional skill. His answer was "I hold a diploma, but if I practised as you do I should only make a bare living, but by giving out that I can cure anything, I am in a fair way to make ray fortune." In a few days after the story became known when his patients de- serted him, and. the local doctors were reinstated in popular favour. This tale illustrates the popular credulity which enables persons possessing shrewd- ness and effrontery to carry on with profit the trade of quack doctors. Mr. and Mrs. Lilly, the "rheumatic doctor and the clever lady doctor" were charlatans, who whatever their igno- rance of the fearful and wonderful construction of the human body were well acquainted with this common weakness of the human mind. Not long ago, we saw these people exciting the admiration of the vulgar in one of the towns they visited by the exhibition of a gorgeous coach drawn by three handsome black steeds, with other attractive paraphernalia, and a band of music, so that thousands followed in their train, and the immense trade they made gave evidence of the effect on popular gullibility, which can be made by a superabundance of outward show. " The Lady Doctor" as she was called, delivered a lengthy rigmarole in French, on her pretended skill and her egotistical ora- tionsixvere heightened in their effect by the loud vocal, translations of an interpreter. Hundreds of pounds must have been extracted from the pockets of the sick poor by these devices. "The Lady Doctor" and her husband were breaking the law in the towns of Lancashire just as much as they offended against the law in Bristol, and we are surprised that the authori- ties allowed them with impunity to carry on their system of deception. These charlatans have visited towns in all parts of England, intensifying ignorance, inflicting cruel pain, on poor people suffering from ailments by raising disappointed hopes of cure, and doing an incalculable amount of mischief; and we are pleased to see that they have at length received a check, so that they will no longer be able to practice their wholesome acts of deception with impunity.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES,
div.p: LOCAL NOTES,

It is a pleasant thing to know that the township of Run- corn will not be put to the expense or excitement of an election for poor law guardians this year, as there are only a sufficient number of gentlemen nominated to fill up the vacancies. Many ratepayers are gratified to know that Mr. William Handley, who has done good work as a poor law guardian in past years, is again elected a member of the Board.

Mr. Lowe, of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, may be censured by some of his fellow labourers upon the Board, for the energy with which he entered into the matter of the two-and-a-half potatoes, but no one who fairly considers the action of this gentleman can help admitting that out of "seeming evil" he has managed to "educe good." It ap- pears that the Local Government Board have decided to descend from the high position which they generally take as great sticklers for everything being done in strict conformity to the regulations of the system of red tape by which their proceedings seem to be principally guided, and to permit the members of the Board who feel they need refreshments after their long journeys and:arduous labours, to enter into an arrangement by which they can purchase what they need from the master of the workhouse. It seems as if the Board of Guardians, as a body, had come to the conclusion that Mr. Lowe has had ample opportunity for airing his grievances, for at the last meeting they opposed any further attempt to let off his surplus steam, and extinguished him, so to speak. But I think it may be taken for granted that Mr. Lowe will, like truth, "rise again," and go on in the course of investigation which he has apparently marked out for himself as part of his life career.

The members of the Widnes Liberal Association may be congratulated on possessing a president such as Mr. E. K. Muspratt, whose knowledge of political matters is exten- sive, and whose purse is ever open when he sees an oppor- tunity of advancing the interests of the cause of peace, retrenchment, and reform. At the annual meeting of the Association which has just been held, Mr. Muspratt took Major Cross, the president of the Widnes Conser- vative Association, to task for the prean of triumph which he had been uttering as to the great things which the sup- porters of what is somewhat impolitely called " the stupid party" had done in the town, and the great gains they could beast in as the result of the last revision. Mr. Muspratt totally denied the accuracy of Major Cross's deductions, and, somewhat facetiously remarked, that it was quite evi- dent the gentleman was a more accurate calculator as an engineer than as a politician! Mr. Martin Taylor, who generally hits pretty hard when he strikes, said that when they scratched a Tory workingman, and get below the skin, they were sure to find a Republican! This is piling Ossa Upon Pelian with a vengeance, and there will no doubt be a sharp reply uttered when the Conservative tribesmen are once more called together.

Runcernians have had a compliment paid them during the week by the election of Mr. Thomas Handley as a member of the Widnes Local Board. I have no doubt that Mr. Handley, who is a gentleman distinguished by much tact and experience of public life, will prove a valuable member of the Board. Let us hope that his position upon it will tend to draw the local authorities of Runcorn and Widnes closer together, so that they may work for the common good of the district on both sides of the Mersey. CANON BABOLAY AND THE RUNCORN IMPROVEDIENr OMMISSIONEES.—The only case which came before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell (chairman) and Mr. Bankes, at the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, was the adjourned summons in which Mr. Brookes, secretary to the Commis- sioners, sued the Rev. Canon Barclay, vicar of Runcorn' for the recovery of £lll Is. Sd., and £2 13s. 10d. interest, for private improvement expenses incurred by that body in the making of parts of Eaton and Fox streets, abutting upon certain land of which the defendant and co-trustees were the owners. The details of the case have been already reported at length in the Examiner.—Mr. W. H.Linaker appeared on behalf of the Commissioners, and said that the defendant had addressed a letter to the Finance Committee stating that in order to settle the difficulty be was prepared to submit to that course. That communication the Board of Commission- ers at that moment were considering, and if the Bench had no objection to wait A short time he would let them know the reault.—Canon Barclay proceeded to read the letter, but Mr. Linaker objected to it being read aloud.—The defendant agreed to hand it to the Bench for their perusal.—After a short conversation with Mr. Ashton, the Magistrates' Clerk, the Chairman said the Bench had had a fortnight to consider the case, and their decision was for the defendant. They did net consider they would be justified in making the order asked for by the Board of Commissioners.—Mr. Linaker : Of course, if my clients feel inclined to test the legal ques- tion you will grant them a case, I presume ?—The Chair- man: We have no objection.

Mr. William Brock;Widnes, has been gazetted a public auditor of friendly societies for this year. Between Runcorn and Weston a very large sand bank has formed, so that the navigation is seriously inter- fered with.
The committee of the Runcona Literary and Mechanics' Institute have received notice that they will be required to vacate the premises they now hold, owing to a change in the tenancy.

WIDNES GOOD TEMPLARS. - On Tuesday evening, a capital meeting in connection with the Samaritan Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Baptist chapel, Nelson-st., Widnes; and followed by a miscellaneous entertainment. FARNWORTH PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL. - On Monday evening, a service of song, called "the children's Messiah," was given by the scholars attending this school, assisted by several members of the Parish church choir. The connective readings were given by the vicar; and during the evening the prizes for regular attendance and good con- duct were distributed to the children.

*PRESENTATION AT RIINCORN.—Mr. Robert Wright, who has held the post of superintendent of the Runcorn Fire Brigade for about two years, was, on Tuesday night, presented by Mr. John Parry, deputy superintendent, with a beautiful silver whistle and chain, on behalf of the members of the brigade. It has been decided to wind up the society known as the Runcorn Naturalists' Field Club, owing to the small attendance of members at the excursions during the past season. The small balance in the hands of the treasurer will be handed over to the Literary and Mechanics' Institute.

WASHINGTON COUNTY COMIT. —A sitting of this court was held on Thursday, before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. An interpleader case of R. Bennett ?). James Walsh was called on, but Mr. Hamilton, barrister? who appeared for Bennett, took exception to the answers given by Mr. Graham who represented Walsh, to the inter- rogatories, aml as His Honour held the application to be a reasonable one tke case was adjourned until next court.

TILE CENSUS—The delivery of the enumeration papers at Warrington was completed on Saturday last. The borough bad been divided into 37 districts, and the enumera- tors commenced and completed the work of collection on Monday. The manner in which the papers were filled up showed a marked advance in the general educational status of the population during the last ten years, and this is one of the most gratifying facts the enumeration has evidenced. The enumerators are to deliver the schedules and enumera- tion books, along with their claims for allowances, on the 11th inst., to the Registrar, Mr. J. C. Sutton, who will, by the 25th inst., forward all householders' schedules to the Census Office.

On Wednesday, the land which it is proposed to purchase for the Infectious Diseases' Hospital at Runcorn, was staked out by Mr. Barker, surveyor to the Commission- ers, and visited by the agent to the Marquis of Cholmond- ley, who will submit a report concerning it for hi s employer's inspection. STARR-BOWICETT SOCIETY FOR WIDNES. On Wed- nesday evening, a meeting was held in Lacey-street Wesleyan Schoolroom, Widnes, for the purpose of forming a Starr- Bowkett society for that town. Mr. Martin Taylor presided. Mr. Starr gave an interesting address on the special advan- tages of the society to working men, as compared with many, if not all, of the present permanent benefit building societies. About 30 members joined at the close, and took up about 80 shares.

--- - CAMDEN BAND OF HOPE, BIINCORN.—At a meeting of this society, at which Mr. S. Pope presided, addresses on the temperance question were given by Messrs. Arthnr Bibby and Mr. T. Faulkner. The treat of the evening's entertain- ment was the dialogue "Miss Burtou's Troubles," which was nicely rendered. The characters were well rendered, and those of cook, coachman, and page boy caused much amusement. Mr. J. B. Clarke accompanied the various songs.

Runcionx Rtmar. SennAiry Atrrnonrrir.—The fort- nightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tues- day, Mr. John Ashton presiding. There were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, W. Pickering, P. Percival W. Whitlow, 11. Neild, 11. Low, R. Ashton, J. Darbyshire, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). A letter was read from the Local Government Board sanc- tioning the payment of £BO to the clerk for his services to the Authority during the past year.—There was 110 other business of public importance.

PRESENTATION TO A YOUNG LADY AT RUNCORN.— On Thursday evening, Miss Nowell, daughter of the Rev. J. Nowell, Superintendent of the Runcorn Wesleyan Cir- cuit, was presented with a very handsome dressing hag and an illuminated address lay her 3unday scholars. A tea meeting was held in one of the class rooms adjoining Brunswick School. The tea was provided by Mr. Moly- neaux, and about 30 scholars at down to it. Afterwards, Mr. John Simpson, on behalf of the sch jars, made the presentation, and in a brief speech expressed his own and their regret at losing Miss Nowell. Mr. Soulby then replied for Miss Nowell, and the roo.n having been cleared of the forms, the party indulged in games for a short time.—Com.

WIDNIIIB LOCAL BOARD ELECrION. —The voting papers were examined at the Local Board offices on Wednes- day by Major Cross, the chairman. The voting was par- ticularly heavy, as will be seen by the return we give below In fact, there has not been so much interest taken in an election in Widnes for some years. The members of the Widnes Owners' and Ratepayers' Association, who for some time past gave taken a very prominent stand on public mutters, and brought their opposition to what they alleged was extravagance and mismanagement on the part of the old members, by waiting upon the Local Government auditor when he made his annual visit, put forward Messrs. S. Sadler, R. Webster. J. Midwood, and J. Shuttleworth, jun., as their bandidates. The Owners' and Occupiers' association were determined that the contest should decide whether the policy of the old members was approved of by the ratepayers or not, and they put forward as their candi- dates Messrs. F. H. Gossage, J.P., E. Carey, and G. I. J. Wells: and also Messrs. W. H. Kershaw and Thomas Hand- ley, of Runcorn. The noMinees of the last named society all came off victorious, which would seem to intimate that the general body of the town's ratepayers are by no means so much inclined to cen- sure the conduct of the Local Board during the past few yeareas has been stated. lt must have been depressing to the committee of the Owners' and Ratepayers' Association to find each of their men at the bottom of the poll, but this was the result of the polling. The following shows the number of votes recorded for each gentleman :—Mr. F. H. Gossage J.P., 2,044; Mr. Eustace'Carey, 1,574; Mr. G. I. J. Wells, 1,563; Mr. Thomas Handley, 1,386; Mr. W. H. Kershaw, 1,346; Mr. Samuel Sadler, 1,248; Mr. T. Shuttle- worth, jun., 1,016; Mr. Richard Webster, 999; Mr. Joshua Midwood, 943. The first five gentlemen were declared elected. After the announcement of the result of the poll- ing, by the Returning Officer, Mr. Handley moved a vote of thanks to Major Cross for the patience and courtesy he had shown whilst examining the papers. Mr. James Rimmer seconded the proposition, which was carried unanimously. Major Cross suitably replied, and the proceedilgs ter- minated.

DELTIC OF S/I1 PHILIP EGEBToN, M.P. Intelli- gence of the death of Slr Philip Egerton, M.P., for West Cheshire, reached his residence, Outten Lodge, Tarporley on Tuesday morning. Sir Philip was, with one exception'' the oldest member of the House. He represented Chester for a brief period prior to 1830, and in 1835 was returned for South Cheshire. When the county was re-arranged, in 1868, Sir Philip was returned for West Cheshire' and he sat for it undisturbed down to the late election, when, for the first time he fought for his seat. He was returned at the head of the poll, receiving 700 votes more than his closest opponent, Mr. Cornwallis West, and over 100 more than his colleague, Mr. Tollemache. The Liberals attributed their defeat to the popularity of their opponent. It is understood that Mr. West will stand again, as he addressed a meeting of Liberals at Crewe so recently as Thursday last. Majer ETerton (who succeeds to the estates, and is at Oulton Lodge) left his father in his usual state of health on Mon- day afternoon. COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS, WARRINGTON.—At this court on Wednesday, before Mr. G. Artingstall, Patrick and Mary, Folan, man and wife, were charged with committing a breach of the peace, at Woolston, on the 16th ult., at 10 o'clock. They were bound over to keep the peace for six mlnths.—Alfred Woodhouse, a young married man, was Hued 205., including costs, for indecently exposing himself, Orford Avenue, on the 31st ult.

j I The weekly meeting of the Board was held on Wednesday. Present—Mr. W. Derbyshire On the chair), the Rev. la. F. Roberts, Major Cartwright, Messrs. Blackhurst, Wallington, Loughlin, Marsh, Longshaw, Brown, Harrison, Winstanley, /Global!, Hall, Gibson, Greenall, Fairhurst, Humphreys, Woolfal I, Appleton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), G. Mackey (master), and C. N. Spinks (medical officer). Mr. Basil Cane, Local Government Boatd inspector, also attended.

TIM STATE OF THE HODSZ. Mr. MACLEY (the master) reported 496 inmates in the house last week; admitted, 10; discharged, 18; total 488 this week, as compared with 485 in the corresponding week of last year. The vagrants relieved during the week num- bered 157, of whom 128 were men, 24 women, and 5 chil- dren. He also reported one case of fever. THE DOCTORS CHARGE,..—THE BOARD IN A DILEMMA. The CLERK, referring to the doctors' charges for inspec- ting the barracks, drew the attention of the Board to Dr. Watkin's letter of the 2nd February, in which he returned the cheque for £3 35., firmly refusing to receive it "in the obnoxious form of a gratuity." He stated that as he had advised them it seemed to him that a paid officer of the Union could only be recompensed by gratuity, bethought he would put the question to the Local Government Board, when he submitted to them the Guardians' proposition on the original resolution that these gentlemen should have a sum of money in addition to that already granted t 0 them. The Board replied as follows:

Eifr,—l am directed by the Local Government Board to ac- knowledge the receipt of your letter of the 10th instant, and to inform you that in pursuance of article 172 of the general order of the 24th of July, 1847, they approve of the payment by the Guardians of the Warrington Union of the sum of two pounds two ehitlings each, to Messrs. J. W. Watkins and R. Sephton, and of the sum of three pounds three shillings each to Messrs. J. H. Gornall and G. W. Joseph, in consideration of the extra services which they rendered in connection with the temporary schools and Workhouse hospital of the Union. With regard to the enquiry contained in the concluding portion of your letter, I am directed to state that, as Mr. Watkins is as dis- trict medical officer, a gratuity, under article 172 of the above. mentioned order, appears to be the only form in which extra remuneration for the services rendered by him can be paid by the Guardians.

Mr.-BrAmunmsr: Exactly. It is just as we have said. The CLERK I have now made out three cheques for these gentlemen, but in face of this letter I await your instructions as to what I must do with Dr. Watkins. Mr. BLACERURST supposed unless Dr. Watkins had the gratuity he could not have the money at all. Inasmuch as Dr. Watkins had objected to having it in that objectionable way, as be termed it, be thought it would be well to ask Dr. Watkins in what other way he thought the Board could pay him. The CLERK, in reply to Major Cartwright, said he had In- formed Dr. Watkins that the money could only be paid as a gratuity, and he got an abusive reply. It was useless for him to send the cheque. The CRAIRMLN said Dr. Watkins was still in the same mind as he was when he wrote this letter, and did not look upon the additional two guineas as a palliating circumstance in the case. Ile thought there was nothing for the Board to do but to keep the money. Mr. BLACKEURST : No; J. do not think I should Send him the money. Mr. WALLINGTON : I object to sending him a cheque. The Cut: I think you should not instruct me to draw a cheque in the face of these words. Mr. BLACICHITRST : Certainly not. Let the clerk com- municate with him. He proposed that the clerk be instructed to do so.
Mr. 13nowle moved that a cheque for £5 58. Od. be for- warded to Dr. Watkins for services rendered.

Mr. HARRISON: And say nothing about the gratuity. Mr. WALL:Nerrow : Dr. Watkins has refused to receive the money as a gratuity, and the Board can pay that monex in no other way. I beg to second Mr.Blackhurst's motion that a letter be writtan to Dr. Watkins, statiug that he could re- ceive the money, and that we can pay the money in no other way than that.

Mr. WOOLFALL supported the motion. Mr. Ham/Isom seconded the amendment. Major .Canrwiamwr thought the Board should simply take the proper course, and remit Dr. Watkins a cheque for services rendered. If be refused the cheque, let him send it back; it would be his own fault. If he accepted the cheque it would be quite right. Mr. BLACKHURST did not see why the Board should be put in such a humiliating position, as to have a cheque returned to them. (Hear, hear.) Mr. WALLINGTON thought an apology was due from Dr. Watkins to the clerk, for his very insulting letter. (Hear. hear.) The amendment and motion were then put to the vote, And the motion was carried.

div.p: RUNCORN POLICE- COURT.
TuunsraY.—Before Mr. James Reynoll4 (chairman) and Mr. S. B. Chadwick.

ALLEGED THEFT OF A LOAF BY AN OLD OFFENDER.— Mary Connor, a middle-aged woman, was charged with having, on the 2nd inst stolen a loaf, the property of Wm. Massey, grocer, Brunswick-strect.—The prosecutor's wife said that about half-past seven, on Saturday night, they had twenty-two 41. b loaves in the shop window, where they had been placed a few minutes before. She went into the kitchen for ten minutes and she heard some one knocking. On going into the shop, she saw the prisoner there, and, after asking for a halfpenny turnip, of which they had not any, she went off without buying anything. She counted the loaves after the woman had gone, and found one missing: The loaf pro- duced was a similar one, and there was a private mark, con- sisting of a branch, upon it. She was confident she did not sell the prisoner one. Whilst prisoner was in the shop i she noticed that she had something bulky n her apron. Prosecutor gave evidence as to inissing the. loaf.—Mary O'Neil, alias Martin, widow, of !VIM-street, said. the prisoner had lodged with her about three months. Prisoner left her house on Satw day night about seven o'clock, and returned in about an hour. She saw P.C. Kelly find the loaf produced in a desk in the back kitchen of her house in which the prisoner kept her provisions. When the prisoner came into the house on Saturday evening, she noticed that she had something in her apron--P.C. Kelly said that on appre- hending the prisoner she stated that she was not at the pro- secutor's shop on the Saturday night. On the afternoon of that day she sent her little girl to fetch a loaf. On her return she asked her where she had *got it, and she said from Massey's.—Prisoner's daughter gave evidence corroborative of her mother's statement; but on being cross-examined by twhhrr she eedh had wdohni tf h so h leo owto_u pd r attoo nt ette tell as ot onroi ems ma ibtot oudt Superintendent Williamson, admitted that her mother had Pe ahse rt oi to the Quarter Se sions for trial. A DISORDERLY WOMAN. —Sarah Smith, who had been convicted eight time previously, was fined 209. and costs, or one month's imprisonment, prisoner having been drunk and disorderly in Cooper-street on the previous night. P.C. Noden proved the case. A DESERTER FROM WARRINGTON.—Martin Maloney was charged with being a deserter from the 92nd Regiment of Foot, stationed at Warrington. The man was apprehended in the street by Sergeant Cashin. The magistrates ordered that the prisoner should be taken back to his regiment at Warrington.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.

Sr. PETER'S CEURCH,Nawrox.—The fifth Lenten sermon by special ministers was preached in this church, on Sunday last, by the Rev. Canon Dodd, of Stretton, the church being well filled. LEC CORE AT THE CATHOLIC HALL, NRWTON.—An in- teresting lecture was delivered in this hall, adjoining the Roman Catholic School, Crow-lane, by Mr. M. F. Duffy, of Liverpool, on "St. Patrick, the patron saint of Ireland." The lecturer, after thoughtfully dealing with his subject, gave some pleasing sketches of the Irish statesman, Daniel O'Connell. There was a large attendance. Mr. Frank McAdam, of Liverpool, presided. A hearty vote of thanks I was awarded to the leeturer and chairman, on the motion of the Rev. James Lennon.

LANCASHIRE HussAm.—The annual inspection of horses, preparatory to the Southport expedition, took place bef3re Colonel W. J. Legh, at Garswood Park, on Saturday. The horses were fully up to the average of previous years. The troop, under the command of Adjutant Reif, fully sustains its efficiency.

EARLESTOWN, ANTI-COMPULSORY VACCINATION LEAGUE. —A general meeting of the members of the above League was held on Wednesday, when there was a very good at- tendance of members present. It having become known that summonses were being issued this week against some 12 or 15 of the oldest defaulters, who, it is expected, will have to appear at the Newton petty sessions, on Saturday, it was resolved to prepare for a vigorous defence, and arrange- ments were made for the active support of such itandidates for election on the Board of Guardians as are favourable to non-compalsion with the vaccination laws. NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS CRICKET AND BOWLING CLUE.— The first ordinary meeting of the season was held at the Pied Bull Inn, on Thursday evening, Mr. John Ball in the chair. It was resolved that, owing to the 111th April clash- ing with other events in the locality, &c., the opening day be delayed until April 23. Preliminary steps were taken in connection with the athletic sports to be held in June. WESLEYAN TEA MEETING.—One of the best and largest society tea meetings in connection with the Brunswick Wesleyan Chapel, was held on Wednesday evening, in the schoolroom of the old chapel. At the after meeting in the Lecture Hall of the new chapel, the Rev. R. Crozier presided, and in a very interesting speech gave an account of the quarterly meeting at St. Helens for the March quarter, which closes the returns for the twelve months preparatory for conference. It is gratifying to learn there is no decrease this year, but a nett increase of .25 in the whole circuit. The future of Methodism in Earlestown promises well, as the tone of the meeting showed a unity of purpose and a determination to work, which is so essential for success in any Christian body. Arrangements are being made for out- door services during the season.

The words "Cocoa" and "Chocolate " are of Mexican origin. "Chocolate" from Chocolatl, the somai made in bruising the Cocoa with sugar. Cacao is the Cocoa of commerce of which Cildbury's Cocoa Essence is a pure preparation.-Inrx.

div.p: THE FEVER 4IOSPITAL.

The CLERIC read a letter from the Local Government Board, acknowledging the receipt of a letter forwarding amended plans of the proposed alterations to the hospital, at the Warrington Union Workhouse, and stating that the Board now approved of the plans under their seal. It must, however, be understood that thisapproval did not relieve the Guardians, or their architect of the responsibility of seeing that the works were carried out with efficiency and economy. The plans were returned, and the writer was directed by the Board to enquire the estimated cost of the works, and out of what fund the Guardians proposed to defray it. The CLERK suggested that the cost be paid out of the revenue account. Major CARTWRIORT : Are you in pretty good feather as you are talking about paying out of the revenue? The CLERK : I think I can pay even MOO this next half. year without you feeling it.

div.head: COUNTY RATE.
div.p: THE COUNTY RATE.

The CHAIRIWCT, alluding to the above rate, said it ap• peared to him it mounted up very fast. The calls from this Union were not much udder £4OOO per annum. It was an easy thing to make a call upon the Union, and an easy thing for the ratepayers to be compelled to ply it, but there was not one word as to the disposition of the county rate. The Guardians had no control whatever over the disburse- ment of the money. They simply made the call, and scarcely knew what it went for; and he wished to state that the call now amounted to nearly £4,000 a year, It was an alarming sum, and seemed to raise the poor rate very much indeed.
TUE ADMISSION OF PAUPER PATIENTS TO THE INFECTIOUS HOSPITAL. . _

The Visiting Commitieers—bCi-oi-a-a—ted that one ef the girls, Catherine McLoughlin, was sent to the hospital on Friday, last week, by order of the doctor, who subsequently gave instructions for her to be removed to the fever hospital. Dr. Gornall refused, however, to admit her without the con- sent of the Sanitary Committee.

The CLERK said Dr. Spinks wished him to read the fol- lowing letter from Mr. Gornall :—"The letter addressed to Mr. Bloomfield ought to have been referred to me. I decline to admit resident paupers from the Workheuse until I receive decisive instructions from the Sanitary Committee." Major CARTWRIGHT asked where the girl was. Dr. Simms: She is in our own hospital. . .

Mr. BIACIMISIRST said it seemed they were in an unfortu- nate position in regard to the hospital. By some red- tapeism or something they objected to admit the case; and he did not see any remedy for it now but to push forward with their new hospital. If the Sanitary Committee had power to refuse to receive pauper cases, it was no use ask- ing them again to admit the case. Perhaps the Clerk could tell them whether they really could object. Mr. HARRISON; Could I ask Dr. Spinks if he has had any further communication from or with Mr. Gornall since that. Dr. SPINKS No.

HARRISON a" i 1 they were supposed to make provi- sion for their own pauper or infectious p ttients, end there- fore the Sanitary Authority of the Corporation no doubt had a perfect right to refuse the case. But he was far from believing that they would have refused it if an application hid been made to them in the first instance, because he had heard the chairman of the Sanitary Commiitee say that their object was to endeavour, as far as they possibly could, to get rid of disease, and, be the patients rich or poor, they would not refuse them admission. Mr. Braciitußsr said Dr. Spinks applied to a man in charge at the hospital. He was told he should make his application somewhere else, but the patient might die in the meantime. It only showed the necessity for proceeding with their own hospital. Major CARTWRIGHT :Am Ito understand that this is not a free hospital ? " " • -

. Mr. HARRISON said the hospital was free to everybody living in Warrington; but the Workhouse was a community in itself, and was deemed to be a community existingoutaide Warrington. Major CARTWRIORT : May I ask the medical Officer . where the case emanated?

Dr. SPINES : The girl has been in the House seven years. Major CARTWR/GHT: She belongs to Warrington? Mr. BLACICHORST : Of course. Major CARTWRIGHT : Has there been a resolution put in the Sanitary Committee's minutes to the effect that the hospital is free? _ . .

HARRISON: Certainly, to every inhabitant of War- rington, but as I said just now the Workhouse is supposed te be a community outside Warrington, and is so treated. Mr. BLACHHURST: They are not inhabitants of Warring- ton? A GUARDIAN: No.
Mr. BtacitnunsT : I never heard such a thing. Dr. SPINICS, in answer to Mr. Harrison, said he made application for admission in the usual way to the superia- tendent of the hospital.

. . - Mr. HARRISON: If yeti had applied to Mr. Gornall I am quite sure he would have received the patient. Dr. SPINES said his object in bringing this forward was to ask the Board to push forward the fever hospital. Mr. WINSTANLEY said if an application was made for ad- mission to the Workhouse such application would be made to the governor and not to the doctor, and why should it not be SO at the infectious hospital? Dr. Spinks applied to governor, and he was the person who should have admitted the patient. It ought not to be left to the whim of Dr. Gornall. It was understood the Sanitary Committee sought for the good of the community to take people from their homes to that hospital, and how much better was it to take' patients from that Workhouse where they had 300 or 400 persons gathered together. Mr. APPLETON thought the sooner the Board made some arrangement with the Sanitary Authority to accept theh Ipatients the better as the Board bad no claim upon them. Dr. SPINES said the Board was not required to make an arrangement if they would get their hospital completed.

• _ Mr. Bastr. CANE said it would be perfectly legal to sub- scribe a sum of money for the use of the hospital if they got ' the sanction of the Local Government Board. It was quite a question whether it would not be right and proper on their part to subscribe to the infectious hospital; and then they would have a claim and right to send a certain number" of patients there. I

The ORA- Fit'iterTh. said a deputation waited upon the Urban Sanitary Authority and they refused to take pauper patients on any terms whatever, lie did not know whether they still refused to do so, or whether it would be wise to take patients to the hospital. Major Ciatrwttioar Th it was before they made it a free hospital. The CLERK: Oh, no. The final answer as only given a few weeks ago.

MR. HALL AND THE awrivaccisravons. Mr. BLACKHURST said he had read some language which was used at an anti-vaccination lecture at Earlestown, which reminded ,him of the language used during the Irish agitation. There was one member of that Board who spoke at that meetmg, and he should like a little explanation from him in regard to some words that fell from his lips. That member said if any gentleman at that Board offered to speak on behalf of anti-vaccination he was immediately put down. He had been a member of that Board two years, and had never yet seen a member who wanted to speak put down. He thought the man who made statements which were damaging to that Board ought to be called upon to retract or substantiate what he had said. The CHAIRMAN said he was glad Mr. Blackhurst had called attention to the matter. He saw in a paper before him that Mr. Hall used these Words: "He could assure the lecturer that if any Guardian got up at Warrington to ad- vocate anti-vaccination views he was at once put down." I He did not know whether that was meant as a reflection upon the Chairman or upon the whole Board, but since he had been a member of the Board he never remembered an anti- vaccinator being put down. He might inform Mr. Hall that he was himself almost an anti-vaccinator. He objected to vaccination unless they got the vaccine lymph from the right source. When that was done he agreed with it. But when the s amine lymph had passed through the human system frequently he did aot agree with vaccinatiqn, so that if Mr. Hall intended his remarks as a reflection upon the Chairman he was decidedly wrong, for he had never put an anti-vaccinator down. He did not remember the ques- tion ever being brought forward. Whether vaccination was right or not it was not their duty to consider. They had simp?y, as a Board of Guardians, to carry out the law, and as soon as the law was changed he was sure the views of the Guardians would be changed. Mr. flaanisos said there was a discussion some time ago on the question 0 vaccination, and he thought Mr. Hall moved a resolution in reference to vaccination. He was quite sure on that occasion Mr. Hall had the patient atten- tion of the Board to every word he said. But he was not going to quarrel with Mr. Hall by reason of the observations he was said to have made at the meeting where this lecturer used very reprehensible language. There were two ways of looking at Mr. Hall's observations. If he did say what was reported of him, be could only say, so far from his regarding that as a reflection upon the Guardians, that if it was a reflection at all he thought it was one that did them great credit, for it showed they were sufficiently en- lightened to be able to discover the absurdity of anti- vaccination. He, therefore, did not take it as a reproach, but felt rather complimented that Mr. Hall made the re- marks he did; and he thought, if they took that view of it, they ought to be glad it was proclaimed that they were not such enemies of the human race as those who would strangle or destroy the process of vaccination. Major CARTWRIGHT remarked that if Mr. Hall had been treated in the same manner as he had he would have had cease of complaint. It appeared to him Mr. Hall was single-handed there, and when all hands were against him it was hard work to weather the storm. (Laughter.) He had no doubt Mr. Hall got on the platform to say some- thing—something strong. (Laughter.) Mr. HALL denied having made the remarks that appeared in The Warrington Examiner. Mr. BLACKIIIIRST : What paper is that you have got , there? _ . _ .

• The CHAIRMAN : The Leigh Chronicle. Mr. Ham, said if those words were to the same effect he must deny having used them. He did attend the meeting, but he did not go there and state what had been represented —that he was immediately put down if he brought the sub- ject of anti-vaccination forward at the Board, because that was not the case. (Hear' hear.) He had the opinion the if the question was brought forward in a legitimate way it would receive fair consideration, so that he could not pos- sibly have said what had been attributed to him. He did say that if Mr. Booth, the lecturer, was to go to the meeting of the Board of Guardians and state what he had stated there, he would find that it was a very different thing to stating it on that platform. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman had treated him on every occasion with the greatest courtesy, and he might say the same of the members of the Board. (Hear, hear.) Mr. WINSTANLEY: If Mr. Hail denies the truth of the statement there is an end of it. THE OFFICE OF OVERSEER.

The CLERK read copy of a memorial which he had re- ceived from the Salford Union praying for the abolition of the office of overseer of the poor, and, on the motion of Major Carrwarorr, the Board decided to forward to Parlia- ment a similar memorial. MR CAE AND THE BOARD.—THE BOARD AND THE PRESS.

Mr. CANE, in addressing the Board, said he was one of those who thought Guardians ought to be elected for longer periods than they were now—(hear, hear): and be hoped be- fore long there would be an alteration of the law by which the gentlemen finding themselves sitting there would be there for three years without being disturbed. He thought the work the Board had done in 1880-1 had done as much or more good than any Boar he was connected with in the War- rington Union. They had.distinguished themselres by a most persevering course of proceeding by which they had enlarged their Workhouse accommodation, and provided for the health and education of the children, which could not be carried on at those premises, by the erection of a separate school which he hoped wauld soon be completed, and in active operation. It might be invidious and almost in- decorous for him to name any individual member who was specially entitled to the thanks of the community for the great interest he had taken in the pigs,—(laughter)—and the vigilance he had exhibited on that occasion. (Hear, hear.) The Guardians had done very well indeed during the past year, and he took the liberty of naming Major Cart- wright especially. Mr. Hartarsow asked might he be permitted to say with what gratification he had listened to the observations which had emanated from Mr. Cane, and inasmuch as the genius of the press had been the means of bringing them into a notoriety which they never deserved, he hoped Mr. Cane's words would have the effect of neutralising the almost false representations that had been made of the conduct of the Board from time to time. He was not blaming the local press. He must say, so far as the local press was concerned, they were indebted to them for having given' as a rule, very faithful reports of the proceedings of the Board. But it was the foreign press who were anxious to get sensational paragraphs in order to get their circulation extended in any way they could, and made remarks about the Warrington Board of Guardians that were highly unjust, very much coloured, and exaggerated to such an extent as might almost be called falsehoods. He was glad to hear the observations from Mr. Cane, as the observations came from an authority who must be respected by everybody who read the words in the newspapers; and be hoped neither Mr. Cane nor any successor he might have would have occasion to express an opinion that should be in opposition to the sentiments he had so well expressed. (Hear, hear.)

, Major CARTWRIGHT said he Was very much obliged to Mr. Cane for his remarks. He had always done his best, and if he had failed he had always tried to do his duty. He might have made himself a little obnoxious or Maar to the members of the Board, but he thought they would bear corn- parison with many ether toards. If people would only read the reports of the proceedings at other Boards of Guardians they would find them ten times worse than the Warrington Board had been. There was no question language had been I used that ought not to have been used, and which had been regretted since, and if he had said or done anything at the Board during the last 12 months to hurt the feelings of the Board he was very sorry. Mr. CANE remarked that it was a great deal better they should have full, free, and unfettered discussion than *at they should be unanimous, and give a perfunctory attention to business. He was glad to come to the Board to listen to the observations made—observatiors characterised by in- telligence and prompted by an honest desire to do the rate- payers the fullest possible service. The CHAIRMAN also briefly replied. nicmgen QP SALARY. Mr. T. J. GARNET-F, relieving officer, having made ap- plication for an increase of salary, Mr. Bttoww moved that his salary be increased to £ll5. Mr. LONGSHAW moved an amendment that the amount be £lOO, and, after some discussion, daring which several members spoke in the most eulogistic terms of Mr. Garnett's conduct, a motion that the salary be increased to £lO5 per annum was carried without dissent. This was all the business. •

LORD BEACONSFIELD'S HEALTH.

IMarked improvement was reported on Wednesday in the I condition of Lord Beaconsfield, but it was not maintained I throughout the night. About three o'clock on Thursday I . morn.n_., the noble earl was seized with another attack of spasms, and 1:!W symptoms were of so disquieting acharacter tint Sir W. aenner was sent for. The bulletin issued 011 Thursday morning stated that the unfavourable symptoms had ' nearly passed away, leaving his lordship not materially worse than prior to the attack. In the afternoon, it was an- nounced that his lordship, though weak, had not lost ground. Thursday night's bulletin stated that his lordship had passed the day free from any distressing sytimtoms, and that his weakness incident to the course of his malady was the chief cause of anxiety.

div.head: IRISH MEMBERS AND THE LAND BILL.
div.p: THE IRISH MEMBERS AND THE LAND BILL.

' A meeting of the Irish members was held on Thursday evening, on the conclusion of Mr. Gladstone's speech, to consider the proposed scheme of land reform in Ireland. It was decided to defer action for the present. RUMOURED RESIGNATION OF THE DUKE OF ARGYLL.
A rumour prevailed on Thursday evening that the Duke of Argyll had resigned owing to a difference of opinion with his colleagues in the Cabinet as to the Land Bill. MR. MACKONOCHIE'S APPEAL.

On Thursday, the House of Lords dismissed with costs the appeal of the Rev. A. H Mackonochie-agaiast the judg- ment of Lord Penzance, in suspending him for three years for disobedience to a monition. MR. GLADSTONE'S HEALTH.

Mr. Gladstone has begun again to take that vigorous walking exercise which was interrupted by his accident, but which is one of the secrets of his marvellous renewals of strength. As soon as he could get away from the House of Commons and his departmental ditties, on Thursday, he was fleeting fast along the London streets. Members who ' stayed until the last, and who walked up Regent-street, met him returning t,) Downing-street at his usual pace. He is still as erect and his step is still. as firm as ever ; but he Shows more signs of weariness after exercise than be did before his accident. The east wind seems to suit him. Strange, is it not, that a wind from the East should brace him and prove so dangerous to Lord Beaconsfield ?

Strut- vex and Mr. Jusrtx MCCARTHY urged the Government to refuse the aid of the police and 'military to carry out unjust demands of Irishlandlords.—Mr. Foamlt said if hon. gen- themen would advise Irish tenants not to resist the law the greatest good would result as it would render force unneces- sary.—Mr. CHAPLAIN said that through the action of the Government in Ireland and the Transvaal Parlizunent would separate for the holidays with a deep feeling of degradation —Mr. GLADSTONE defenJed the conduct of the Government and in severe terms replied to the observations of Mr. Chap lin.—After some further discussion, the motion for the adjournment was agreed to.

SAD STREET ACCIDENT AT WARRINGTON.—On Thurs- day afternoon, a boy named Fred k. William Greenwood, 10 wars of age, and his brother, Albert John, two years of 'age, were seriously injured in Factory-lane, near Bank Quay Station, Warrington. The boys were standing near a funeral coach in the street, when an engine which was standing in Mr. Westwell's coal yard, whistled. The horses ‘vere startled and took off, and the lads were knocked down, the coach passing over the thigh of Albert, and the body of Frederick.. The buys were immediately conveyed to the Infirmary, and under the care of the house surgeon are pro- grrssing -- • as well as can be expected.
