TRINITY COLLEGE, LONDON. Sir,—The Trinity musical examination being now antici- pated, and a considerable amount of anxiety being felt, by both parents and teachers generally, as well as by the young people who may sit, allow me to call the attention of your readers to the fact that certain local prizes given by gentlemen in the neighbourhood will be competed for, and adjudicated by the college authorities. These, it is hoped, Will be still further increased as the time draws nearer, and will be in addition to those offered by the college for general competition, which Sir J. Benedict will adjudicate. As the hon, local secretary, I shall be most happy to receive any further kind offers of assistance from gentlemen or ladies who are wishful to promote local effort, whether for choirs, or schools, or families, in this department of education.— Yours, &c., JOHN BUCKLEY, F.R.G.S., 4m. The Academy, Winsford. CHESHIRE FARMERS' GRIEVANCES. Sir,—l notice in your last the letter of an " Old Woman" satirising the courage of Cheshire fanners, who had met to organise agitation on behalf of fixity of tenure, fair rents, and free sale, and am only surprised at their long continued suffering, without a murmur, for the last 3 years. Nearly all trades during the last 20 years have corabined together, and the colliers have followed snit in the direction. The wages of all classes have been considerably raised, and if the tenant farmers of this country would do the same they need not fear being, able to secure fixity of tenure, fair rents, and free sales, and they would be in a position to defy the competition et the world. They should aim only at making the very best butter and the very best cheese; which would command high and remunerating prices, and amply pay for extra care and attention. There are many widows who are farmers in Cheshire, and these would do well to agitate for women's rights, with the power of voting for members of the Commons House of Parlia- ment. The absence of this nualificltion is the chief reason why landlords object to widows holding farms. The rents of many villages in Cheshire have been raised 10 and 12 per cent. per annum within the last ten years, and the only return has been about 10 per cent, for one half-year only, sufficient to induce all farmers to direct their eyes towards the far west, or to Australia, or New Zealand, where free- holds can be bought at the annual rents paid in this country by tenant farmers. They want the Ulster Tenant Right adopted in England, and I would whisper in their ears the words of Milton—" Awake, arise, or be for ever fallen."—Yours, JUNIUS.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
The last meeting of this Board was heli on Thursday, Mr. B. Marsh presiding.

INILATES IN THE nouns. The MASTER reported that the number of inmates in the house was 469, as against 496 the previous week, and 492 in the corresponding week of last year. THE NEW CIIAPEL. A letter was read from the Local Government Board replying to the letter of the Guardians respecting their pro- posal to erect a chapel at the Workhouse, and the Board requested that the Guardians furnish them with a plan of the Workhouse and premises showing the intended position for the chapel. The CLERIC said he would send a copy of the tracing. FIRE AT TAR WORKHOUSE. The MASTER reported there had been a small explosion of gas in Mr. Latimer's room, on the 24th March, which appeared to have be3n caused by two or three hot cinders. The damage done was small. A EFFRACTORY PAUPER. The Mamie reported that a young man named Andrew Flemington had, absconded from the Workhouse, and returned over the fence atnight, after the house was locked up. As he was very drunk, he was handed over to the police, and sent to prison for seven days. MIXING A POST VORTlnet PKAIKINkTION WITHOUT PERMISSION. The CLERK said be wrote to the Liverpool Vestry asking for an explanation respecting the post mortem examination made upon a child of one bf the inmates named Farrell at Kirkdale schools. He had received a letter in reply, saying that they had investigated the matter. As regarded the discolouration noticed upon the face of the body, the com- mittee could only suppose that it was due to some obscure post mortern action occurring in the body itself, as they were satisfied that the child neither fell out of bed nor was subjected to violent treatment during life. The Vestry Committee regretted that the feelings of the mother should be hurt by any unnecessary examination of the body, but thry were assured by the medical officer that in this pare ticular case the examination was desirable, the result prov- ing that the lungs were tubercularly affected. The Guardians thought that was a satisfactory answer, and the subject dropped, PROPOSED ALTERATIONS AFFECTING THE COLLECTION OF RATES. The Finance Committee's minutes stated that it was re- solved the relieving officers' applications for an increase in their salaries be deferred to a future meeting; as also the salary to be assigned to Drs. Hall and Melicoll, district medical officers; that the present Widnes collector's dis- trict be divided, Whines forming one district with Mr. Rigby as collector at a salary of £175 per annum; Bold, Cronton,Ditton, and Whiston to form a second district to be termed the Whistan district; that a collector be appointed at a salary of £BO per annum. Mr. MEADOWS said that Mr. Rigby, the collector, had made the excuse that the work was too much for him, and that he was obliged to pay £4O a year out of his own pocket for assistance. Seeing, therefore, that he had the largest district, they thought it advisable to make the alteration mentioned in the minutes. At present his salary was £l5O a year, towards which Widnes pail £lOO. They now recom- mended that his salary be £175. Mr. FIDLER said the overseers and the leading inanufac- turetS of Widnes were agreeable to the change, and also wished to have two rates in the year. That meant more work, and the extra £25 was very little. Mr. MKerirrws said if the work could be clone properly it would be a great saving, and he agreed with the recommen-

elation. Mr. TYRFIZ believed Mr. Rigby would bare quite enough to do to collect money in Widnes alone. He thought the better alteration would be to take Rainhill from the Prescot district, and restore it to its old district—Widnes. Preseot, Whiston, and Iluvton would be velj, compact. Mr. LEATFIERBAEROW would protest most most strongly against Whiston being tacked on to any of the little town- ships as Whiston had, up till now, managed very well. Mr. LEIGH objected to the increase in salary as too much. Mr. TIMER moved that the minute relating to the division of the districts being referred back, and the. motion was carried,

TER SCHOOLS 4:117ESTIo0l. A deputation consistink of the Rev. T. Chambers, Mr. Leatherbarrow, Mr. Meadows, and Mr. Tyre, waited upon Mr. Hibbert, of the Local Government Board, en Monday, on the question of the new schools. The Board, notwith- standing the representation of the Guardians that the children were well cared for at Kirkdale,,had insisted upon the work being carried out. The Rev. T. CHAMBERS now said the deputation had been successful in their object, and had, obtained the sanction of the Local Government Board to pay £l5O to Messrs. Weeks and Hughes for the plans. They also obtained sanction to keep the children at Kirkdale for two years, and d the end of that time to wait upon the Board again. It was decided that the plans be returned to Messrs. Weeks and Hughes, and that £l5O be offered to them as a dottier. Mr. Snowlf responded. He was glad to hear the Secretary for Foreign Affairs say that the Opposition bad acted in a vigorous, fair, and generous manner. It was their duty to I act in fair spirit towards anything brought forward by the Ministry. The Opposition did not exist for the purpose of obstruction, but to discuss everything in a fair spirit. If that policy was pursued it should tend to good, and he trusted that in their deliberations they would not be swayed bal

• faction. Mr. Moss proposed "The borough and corporation of St. - 'Helens." lie caosed congiderable amusement by describing one of Nsop's fables which gives an account of a war between the bea.ts and the birds and of the bat being always on the side of the victors. The bat he likened to Liberal- - Conservatives, and he said they had no bats in their society. ' Adverting to the present meeting place of the society as not . being altogether suitable, he threw out a hint that the cor- poration might find the society better and more central

-quarters. The toast was duly honoured, and the glee party sang " Lovely night." The MAYOR briefly returned thanks, and remarked that as • he bad been mach pleased with the evening's proceedings he hoped to have the pleasure of meeting them all again there. (Applause.) Mr. Ataxy, in a humonrorivand tellinaspeech, proposed "The ladies." to which Mr. T. Gi.ovmt (Secretary for the Colonies) responded. The National Anthem was sung by the glee party, and the proceedings terminated.

REPORT OP TRH jtilaGES OJ TIM WIGAN ELECTION Prryrume.—The report of Justices Grove and Bowen (pre- sented to the House of Commons, on Monday) as to the = Wigan election petition trial says:—" We report that at the conclusion of the said trial we determined that Francis Sharpe Plawal, being the member whose election and return were complained of in the said petition, was not duly elected or returned, and that his election and return were and are wholly null and void- on the ground of bribery by agents, and we do hereby certify in writing such determination to you. And whereas charges were made of corrupt practices having been made at the said election, we, in further pur- suanee of the said Acts, report as follows :—(a) That no - corrupt practice wal proved to have been committed by or with the knowledge or consent of any candidate at such elec- tion. (b) The following persons have been proved at the triaLguilty of the corrapt_practice of bribery :---Thomas Scott and Edwin NPLoughland. (e) That there is reason to believe that corrupt prsttices have extensively prevailed at the elect-lonia the ißloegh of. Wigan to which the said petition relates." 7-crir - - -
Two esparto grass sheds on East Moors, Cardiff, have hers consumed by fire. The damage is estimated at 117,000.

div.head: WARRINGTON TO COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TO COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday evening at the Town Hall. The Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Holmes, Kean, Web- ster, Harrison, Chandley ; Councillors Platt, Brown, Wool- fall, Taylor, Barker, Dixon, Fairclough, Broadbent, Percival, Monks, Litton, Jeans, Whittle, Francomb, Ridgway, Green- all, Ashton, Burgess, Crosfield,, Milner, Sutton, Hind, Woods; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), C. Chorley . (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), and J. Paterson (gas manager). HARMSTON'S CIRCCS. The MAYOR said he had had a letter from the proprietos of the circus in Warrington. He wanted the patronage of . the mayor, aldermen, and town councillors of Warrington for his circus for some convenient day. He (the Mayor) 11 believed the circus was carried on in a very proper manner. [ Be had not been himself yet, but some of his friends had told him it was well worth seeing. As Mayor, he did not know whether he could tack on the whole of the Corpora- tion. 'That was for the Council to say. (Laughter.) Councillor Perm The Corperationwill be glad to follow where the Mayor leads. (Laughter.) Councillor BROADBENT said if Alderman Harrison took part in the performance they would all go. (Laughter.) The MAYOR said Mr. Harmston called upon him a few weeks ago, but he said he wanted to see how the circus was conducted, and if it was conducted properly he would be glad to give hie patronage. Mr. Harrnston's application seemed to meet with the ap- proval of the Council. WATCH COMMITTEE.—THE APPOINTMENT OF AUDITOR. The minutes of the Watch Committee comprised the fol- lowing recommendatiohs :—That an order for constables', sergeants', and inspectors' caps be accepted. That Conn- ' cillor Woolfall be requested to audit the accounts of the clerk to the borough justices. That the estimate of expen- diture for the half-year commencing 26th approved: Watch department: r elice,£lle3ch ,7 duct Government grant, £786 2s 9d; Medical officer's salary, A, coals, gas, water, incidental, &c., £l7B 45; total £964 6.3 512 de- duct 1881, be 6d ; 93. Fire engine department: Firemen's wages, materials and repairs, &c., £132 us 6d. That the tender of Messrs. fireball and Son for cleansing and colouring the bridewell and premises be accepted. It was resolved that the question of the supply of water for fire purpoees be referred to the General Purposes Committee, and this committee recom- mend that the Town Clerk be empowered to obtain the opinion of counsel upon the exact position of the Corpora- tion with the Waterworks Compare-. The Borough Treas. surer reported that he had received from Her Majesty's Paymaster General the sum of £1,533 20 103 for half-pay and clothing of the police for the year ended 29th Septem- ber, 1880. It was recommended that a reel and stand be ordered for lase at the police office. The MAYOR moved the confirmation of the minutes, and referring to the resolution in reference to the Waterworks Company, said bethought it a very proper resolution, as in soffte parts of the town they were sadly in want of a sufficient quantity of water for working the fire engines. Alderman Ilanuesoer seconded the motion. Councillor Demos said he would oppose the recommendation as to Councillor Wooltall auditing the accounts of the clerk to the borough justices, and especially after what had taken place during the last six weeks. He thought after the con- 'duct Councillor Woolfall had exhibited during the last six weeks, a stand ought to be taken against it. It was desirable, he thought, that some one outside the Council should be appointed to do the work. Councillor Woomet : Perhaps Mr. Dixon will explain what he means? Alderman HOLMES did not know whether Councillor Dixon was going to propose an amendment, but he had no doubt Mr. Woolfall would be glad to be relieved of the work if Mr. Dixon would undertake it. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Woolfall had audited these particular accounts for many years in an exceedingly satisfactory manner, and he had no idea of passing a covert censure upon Mr. Woolfall, as would be implied in the carrying out of Mr. Dixon's suggestion. Councillor WOOLFALL said he should have very grea pleasure indeed in tendering his resignation, if any other member of the Council would undertake the duty. It was * duty that he did not care abeut. Alderman WRBSTER drew attention to the fact that there was no amendment before the Council. i The MAYOR observed that Councillor Dixon had merely made.a passing remark. • , Coulacillor BROADBENT said he did not know what had been referred to that night, but he had the feeling, which was probably ?hared by the members of the Council, that they were very .much indebted to Mr. Woolfall for under- taking the duty of auditing these accounts. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were confirmed without dissent. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. THE POSTAL ARRANGEMENTS. - At a meeting of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee it was resolved that the following plans be ap- proved :—Plans of alterations and additions to house in Bold-street for Dr. Starkey Smith. Plans of 19 new houses and stables at Latchford, for Mr. S. Reynolds. Plans of additional rooms to the People's College, Arpley-street. Plan for new wall for Mr. Thewlie, Knutsford-road. Alteration , in plans of 8 cottages in Chorley-street, for Mr. John Platt. —lt was recommended that the following estimate of ex- penditure for the half-year commencing 26th March, 1881, be approved :-701 street lamps at 275., £946 75.; purchase of land for street improvements, £100; total, £1,046 U.—lt was resolved that the committee take no action in the matter of houses already built upon chemical waste, and that a number of new streets be adopted. Councillor Betoeneoerr proposed the adoption of the minutes, and stated that the naming of the streets and courts, and the numbering' of the houses throughout the town' had been completed. Councillor nem seconded. Councillor Digo& said the Postmaster saw him a few days age and wished him to use his influence with the Council to see if it was not possible to have letter boxes put in the front doors of the houses. There had been great complaints in many parts of the town of the delay in the delivery of letters. He would be glad if the matter was made known through the Press, as if all the respectable houses in town had letter boxes it would greatly facilitate the delivery of letters. Alderman HOLMES thought Conncillor Dixon's sugges. tion a goad one, and said if the Committee had any power to carry out they would use it. The MAYOR said the Committee had no power to take action and all they could do was to draw attention to the matter. ' Councillor Weterres drew ottention to the non-collection of letters on Sundays from the pillar-box opposite Trinity Church, and remarked that he thought it was a hardship for people to have to carry their letters all the way to the post-office, as:lat present. He did not see why the box could not be cleared about nine o'clock on Sunday evenings. The MAYOR thought if a representation on the subject were -made to the Post-office authorities they might be induced to alter their present arrangements. The minutes were adopted. THE PAYING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE AND THEIR ESTIMATE. The Paving and Sewerage Committee recommended that the plans for the forming and paving Victoria-street and part of Orchard-street, from line marked A.B. on plan to Church-street, be approved, and that the Town Clerk serve thenecessary notices to require the owners or occupiers of property adjoining such streets to pave, flag, and channel such street; and that the footpath on the east side of Factory- lane, from Bank Quay Bridge to end of the building opposite Messrs. Robinson, Son, and Skinner's works, be curbed and tiled.—On the 14th March, it was recommended that the .estimate of expenditure for the half-year commencing the 26th March, 1881, amounting to £3,030, be approved.—lt was recommended that the plan sbbmitted by the borough surveyor for the new pipe sewer in Hamilton-street, off Battersby-lane be approved; that the question of the supply of water for fleshing sewers and other purposes from the Warrington Watet works Company, and also the question as to the taking up of roads by the company, be referred to the General Purposes Committee, and that the Town Clerk be empowered to obtain the opinion of counsel upon the exact position of the Corporation with the company.—lt was re- commended that the tenders of Messrs. R. Turner and Sons, Of Heywood, for the construction of pipe sewer in Dallam- I lane and Kerfoot-street, be accepted. Alderman KEAN, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said lie did so with mingled feelings. It had generally afforded him great pleasure to do so, but certain circumstances had arisen which placed him in a difficulty. They were all aware that things Iffid taken place that would necessitate a very heavy improvement rate for the next half-year. The estimated expenditure for the half-year amoanted to £3,030. The committee bad been content for many years to,accept what he might designate the residue of other contmittees with a view to keep down the improve- ' ment rate to is. 3d. in the pound. But when they found that the Sanitary Committee alone wanted over 15,600, and that a rate of is. ad. in the pound only produced £6,000, it was evident, if the paving and sewerage department was to be of any use, that the committee must form an independent estimate. It had been a matter of surprise both inside and outside the Council that a Is. 9d. rate should be required for ' the current half-year. It occurred in this way—the Sani- tary Committee no doubt felt that the claims upon them were increasing, but he was not aware, until be got figures, that they had during the last three years exceeded their estimated expenditure by upwards of £5,000. In 1879 the estimated expenditure was £5,503, and the actual expendi• ture £8,855; in 1880 £5,802 and £7,438 respectively, and in 1881 £6,533, as against £8,620, making. fl total overspent of £5,069. He did not give these figures in order to complain of what the sanitary Committee had done, but it was -pos- sible they had been a little at fault. Certain contrivances and inventions had been introduced by other towns in this particular department, and it was just possible that had the committee waited until the result of the various experiments had been proved, they might not have been plunged into such a heavy expenditure as they were now called upon to provide for. In addition to this they had made use of their borrowing powers, in connection with the,new Infection.. Diseases Hospital, to the extent of £13,000. He was told there was a further need of expenditure to complete a extensions at Longford; and whether it would be win to pause and make the best of the existing positioe or go forward was the question requiring consideration He had also been curious enough to examine the • expendi. tore of the Paving and Sewerage Committee. He found thar 1 in 1879 they spent £5,584 out of an estimated expen iture of £6,500, showing a saving of £916. In 1880 the esti ated expenditure was £3,400, and the actual expenditure, £ ~888;

minutes. Councillor BROADBENT said it seemed from what the chairman bad stated that the arrangement which had hitherto" prevailed of an important committee like the Paving and Sewerage taking, so to speak, the leavings or residue of other committees was a very bad one, and he thought the sooner it was altered the better. Each com- mittee should act independently, and estimate the expendi- ture it thought necessiry to incur for the benefit of the town. He fancied the town was suffering at present from the plan which had been in operation, as he knew that the members of the Paving and Sewerage Committee and the Borough Surveyor would, if they conld see their way, advise the paving of certain streets with sets instead of putting on macadam. The experience of the committee and all statis \ - tics went to prove that where streets were somewhat flat and damp, it was more economical to pave with sets than to lay macadam. They were obliged by the present injurious finan- cial arrangement to be penny wise and pound foolish, and he therefore hoped the Council generally would acquiesce in the new arrangement. Councillor CROSFIELD asked the Town Clerk whether he had vet received counsel's opinion as to the position of the Corporation and the Waterworks Company. • The Towle CLERK replied that he bad not. He only had instructions the previous week. Councillor JEANS sad the observations made by Alderman Kean and Councillor Broadbent brought afresh to his mind what bad very often passed through it before, namely, that the working departments did not give the Council generally sufficient control ever the expenditure of the borough. Many of them merely saw the figures presented, and were asked to vote large sums of money for purposes which they knew very little about. He thought it would be more satisfactoty if some arrangement were made whereby the members generally could exercise more efficient control over the ex- penditure of the respective committees. He did not know much about the working of the committees, and, therefore, spoke with spume degree of diffidence. The Ill Avon remarked that Councillor Jeans was probably not aware that every member of the Council could make himself acquainted, if he choose to look at the minutes, with the expenditure they proposed to incur. Alderman liormas was glad the committee had brought forward an independent estimate, and wished to know whether they had keen correctly advised in the one proposed for this half year. There could be no doubt that the influ- ence of well-paved streets upon the general health of the town was very beneficial—(hear, hear)—and he thought the committee ought to be encouraged in the future to bring forward an estimate which would be amply sufficient for their requirements. When a change of Govern- ment was imminent some years ago,, it was said they were going to be economical by starving the public services. He was afraid that this kind of economy had operated somewhat prejudicially for the Paving and Sewer- age Committee, and they had not been able to do so much in the way of paving as they might have otherwise wished to undertake. Ile regretted exceedingly the increased ex- ' penditnre in the borough, but it seemed it could not be avoided. Alderman KEAN, referring to what Alderman Holmes said about starving the department he represented, remembered on one occasion when they proposed to vend only £1,200 Councillor Milner asked what they could do with it. His reply was that they must cut theircoatacco d wouldradningtot nheior cloth. They had acted upon that principle, doubt have continued doing so in order to keep the rate at is. 3d. in the pound; but when they found the other com- mittees jumping over the line to the extent indicated, the- Paving and Sewerage Committee thought it advisable to have an independent estimate, and they should do the same in future. The committee had great anxiety in regard .to macadam, for which they found they were paying nearly one thousand pounds Per annum. Macadam was of very ttle use now in Warrington. The minutes were then passed. seam, ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

The minutes of the above committee contained the inspec- tor's report, which stated that 100 cases had been enquired into by the Board of Guardians, and se.hool fees allowed to 195 children. Thirty-four cases had been taken before the magistrates, when fines were inflicted in 23 cases, 6 ad- journed, 3 ordered to industrial school, 1 ordered to the workhouse, and 1 warrant ordered. Sixty-three eeees were brought before the committee and dealt with. The following extract from the report of the inspector was ordered to be entered upon the , minutes :—ln my last report I mentioned that it was my intention in the future to bring before your committee parents wilo regularly—three or four times every week— keep one of their children at home for nursing purposes or cleaning the house, and other duties of a domestic character. The children retained for such purposes are generally girls, from 10 to 13 years of age. Many of these girls fail to make the necessary number of times in attendance to qualify them for examination in consequence of being kept from school so much to perform household duties. lam con- vinced from my daily observations that any latitude given in these nursing cases only encourages indolence on the part of the parent, and in my daily rounds amongst the working class the order for the day seems to be the husband working and the wife out gossiping. It was recommended that the following estimate of expenditure by this commit- tee for the half-year commencing 26th March; 1881, be approved :—lnspectors' salaries, £94 12s'; maintenance of lbws at industrial schools, £l2; sundry charges, £l5; total, £l2l 12s. Aletter was received from a conference recently held at Manchester representing several School Boards and School Attendance Committees, seeking the co-operation of this committee in obtaining an amendment of section 10 of the Elementary Education Act, 1876, so as to transfer from Poor Law Guardians to the local athorities the duty of paying school fees of children whose parents, not being Paupers, were unable by reason of poverty to pay such fees. It was recommended that the committee co-operate with the Conference in endeavouring to effect the object of the reso- lution. Alderman Weesrert moved the confirmation of the minutes, and referring to the conference of School Boards and School Committees, said they considered it was desir- able a change shauld be made in section 10; and the com- mittee had undertaken to co-operate to try to obtain the object wished for. (Hear, hear.) Councillor DIXON seconded the passing of the minutes. He hoped that the payment of school fees would be taken onto! the hands of Boards of Guardians and left with the local authorities. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were agreed to. ' MUSEUM COMMITTEE. —THE FREE LIBRARIES AMEND- MENT BILL. The minutes comprised the following report of the Curator for 'February :—Visitors to the museum 2.602, a decrease of 434; volumes issued to subscribers 2.726, an ' increaee of 583; readers 1,035, a decreese of 227. The committee had discussed the Bill to consolidate and amend the law relating to free libraries, and recommended the Council to petition against the Bill upon the ground that it was decidedly prejudicial to the administration of the public free libraries, that it would rather retard than facilitate efforts which may be made for the establishment of other free libraries; that the defective clauses were too numerous to be amended, and that legislation should be deferred until opportunity had been given to those who had practical ex- per whatie nme ea ni in etrh theyew o rdkei ne mg eodf tthheemetxoi srteign tgi rAe catrns e to d msuggest in Alderman WEBsTEn,.in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said that the committee objected very strongly to the Bill in its present form. The Bill was so ill-considered, and contained so may objectionable clauses, it was thought it would require consideration by a committee appointed from the mei.ebers of the free libraries, that they might ar- rive at such a conclusion as would tend to the formation of a Bill that would really be of service. Councillor BROAMEENT seconded. Alderman HOLMES would like to know whether the Com. miteee took the oppottnnity of purchasing some of the im- portant Parliamentary, reports that were published. A corn- mission had been recently appointed on the agricultural question and their report was interesting, and he should like to know whether the committee had at any time purchas6l snob books. It was important that such books should be obtained for persons who might want to consult them. The Maxon bad no doubt the able chairman of the com- mittee, Mr. Beamont, and the members had very carefully, gone into the question of the free libraries. He did not think they could do better thanleave it in their hands. War- rington was one of the first towns to have a free library, and he should be sorry to see anything done to retard the usefulness of it. Alderman WEBSTER said under the Bill they would, like Boards of Guardians, have to consult the Local Govern- ment Board about everything they did. That was most objectionable, and of itself watt sufficient to induce them to oppose the Bill. (Hear, hear.) In answer to Alderman Holmes, he might say that the committee did purchase Par- liamentary documents, but he was unable to say whether the particular document named was in the library. The minutes were passed, and on the motion of the MAYOR, the seal of the Corporation was affixed to the petition. THE MARKETS COMMITTEIt AND THE LETTING OF THE STALLS AND Mors. The minutes of the Markets Committee comprised a re- commendation that the following estimate of -expenditure for the ensuing half-year be approved :—lnspector's wages, £97 10s.; salary of inspector of weights and measures, £2O ; s9id O rai.e;e, L clothing3o; further for inec- sp sum wages of weighing officer, market hall, £l3; wages of weighing officer, Brielge Font. Ll tors, £11; rates and taxes..£6s ; gas, water, and coals, £6O; maintenance of buildings, £25; nn required for market extensions, £100; total, £44l.—Also report of the Markets Inspector that he had visited live market towns according to instructions, viz.—Wigan, St. Helens, Northwich, Stockport, and Bolton, and he found that in all these places drapery and other manufactured goods were allowed to be sold in the troarkets.—At a meeting held

div.head: THE_ EXAMINER,
div.p: THE_ EXAMINER,

and in 1881, £4400 as against £4,881, giving a total for three years of £14,300 estimated, and £15,353 • actual expendi- ture, or a sum of £1,053 overspent by the Paving and Sewerage Committee. Thus, both the departments were a little at fault. But the reason was this, the Sanitary depart- ment so far exceeded their estimates that the Paving and Sewerage department was in a measure starved, and they were compelled to overrun the coestable. It might be very necessary that sanitary matters should be carried out in a way that would prove most beneficial to the town, but it was a question when there was no epidemic whether the staff at the hospital might not be reduced. He was disposed to save money at a time when there was no serious sickness in the town. (Hear, hear.) He might be excused for yen. turing to allude to what might be regarded as the special ork of the Sanitary Committee, but it was so much linked in with the work of his own department that he could not very well avoid reference to it. Councillor WOOLFALL seconded the confirmation of the

an the 28th March, it was resolved that no alteration be made In the present market arran-e,ements, and that the seven new shops under the new market shed be let subject to the fol- lowing conditions :—That the shops be let free of all local rates, that ne shop be let to a butcher or fishmonger, that the tenants provide their own meters and pay for their own gas. Alderman CHANDLEY moved the confirmation of the minutes, and remarked that a great deal had been said and written on the subject of the letting of the stalls in the market. It was considered that an injustice had been done to the shopkeepers and ratepayers in the borough by letting stalls at such small rates. With a view to paying every res- pect to the complaints made by individuals the Committee thought they would investigate the position of things as they existed in other markets; and they therefore instructed their Inspector to visit five of the neighbouring towns as ; near the size of Warrington as he could find, to ascertain the rate at which the shops and stalls were let, with a view to I guide the committee. The report was before the Council, from which the committee concluded that they were acting judiciously as to the rates charged, and saw no reason to make any alteration. A ratepayers' association had been formed, he believed, in Warrington, to watch the interests of the ratepayers and the public generally. He should be delighted if the association could do. anything to cause him to pay something less in the pound than he was now pav- ing. As to the letting of the shops he might publiclerstate that they had no desire as a committee to erect shops to compete with other tradesmen in the town. Their shops were built originalty as a screen to preteet the market people from the cold west winds. They formed the screen into shops to snit the convenience of those who might want them, and not for the advantage of the committee. They had been let by auction, and, they considered, satisfactorily to the borough financially. As to only payingfive percent. to the ratepayers, that was all nonsente. He could assure the Council and the public that they held very good cards in their hands, but they did not feel disposed to show them publicly. Councillor LITTON seconded. Councillor SUTTON asked whether the tenants of the various shops in the towns referred to paid rates as well as rents kw the shops they occupied. Alderman CHANDLEY said he believed the Town Clerk would advise that the rating of stalls was illegal. There was no rating in the towns from which they had made per- sonal enquiries. The minutes were confirmed. THE EXPENDITURE OF THE SANITARY COMMITTEE.—THE LONGFORD DEPOT AND THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOS- PITAL—MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT. The minutes of the Sanitary Committee comprised a recommendation that the following estimate of expenditure by this committee for the half-year commencing 26th March, 1881, fie approved :—Night soil department, £1,978 ; scavenging ditto, £1,270; working expenses at Longford, £6OO 15s.•' amount required for completion'of extensions at Longford Depot, £1,240; hospital department, £600; total, £5,688 15s.—It was resolved that the question of the supply of water for sanitary purposes be referred to the General Purposes Committee, and this committee recommend the Town Clerk be empowered to obtain the opinion of counsel upon the exact position of the Corporation with the Water- works Comnany.—lt was recommended that the Town Clerk write to Colonel Mansergh, the commanding officer of the 4th R. L. Militia, calling his attention to the overcrowding of houses during their training in the borough; that the tender of Mr. George Helsby for alterations to night-soil van be accepted; that a grey cart mare be purchased from Mr. William Beswick, of Arley; that the Town Clerk serve fresh notices upon the owners of the Blue Lion Yard, off Mill-street, requiring them to pave, flag, and channel such yard, and that the Town Clerk be empowered to engage counsel and take all other necessary proceedings before the magistrates to enforce the compliance with such notices; that a sample of manure manufactured at Longford Depst be submitted to Dr. Voelcker for his complete analysis and report thereon; that the annual report of the Medical Officer of Health be adopted. Councillor Moems, in the absence of the chairman, moved the confirmation of the minutes of the committee. From the remarks made by Alderman Kean and others, the Council intended to make out that the Sanitary Committee were a great spending cornmittee—(hear, hear,)—the extravagant committee of the Council. He was not going to deny the statement that they werea great spending committee, because the figures presented indicated that their expenditure was the largest of any committee of the Council. But if that was so, it was because the departments entrusted to their management requiied the largest expenditnre,and would, be thought, continue to require a very large expenditure from year to year. Alderman Kean had referred to the excess of expenditure over that estimated, and he (Councillor Monks) was not in a position to deny that the committee had ex- ceeded their estimates by the amount named. If it was so, it was because the work of the committee had grown on their hands. But it should be borne in mind that it had been done with the express sanction of the Council. Alder- man Kean had asked whether the committee could not pause and stand still with their new system. There was an old adage to the tffect that it would never do to swop horses in crossing a stream, and in the change from one system to another, they could not stand still. Having changed they must go on, and trust to results so far as the new system was concerned. The committee must ask the indulgence of the Council till the eystembadgot fairly into workingopemtion. With the limited experience the committee had had, they must say that so far on the whole they, had reason to be satisfied. Councillor Mtrame seconded the motion. He could only confirm every word which had been said by Councillor Monks. The Sanitary Committee had taken in hand one of the most difficult questions that had ever eneaged the atten- tion of the Corporation. They had put 'down complete machinery at Longford, which in other towns had been proved in detail. The result was in almost every respect eminently satisfactory, and the only parts where they had reason to be dissatisfied were parts where everyone com- mencing a new manufactory must expect to be troubled: They were already beginning to save money, and he hid no doubt that what Mr. Monks had said would be carried out, and that they would reduce the expenditure very materially. His object in making the remarks he did was simply to show how they were drawn from the system they adopted as a committee into an independent system. He was told that gentlemen from other towns had visited Longford, and examined the system, and confessed that in Warrington it was more advanced than anywhere else. (Hear, hear.) The

Borough Surveyor assured them that he believed it was a ' perfect success so far; and on that point he was quite satis- fied.. The committee borrowed money for 50 years. Councillor PLATT as another member of the committee, objected to Mr. Whittle's remarkable statement. Had he taken the trouble to read Mr. Gornall's very valuable eport he would probably have Come to a different opinion. With regard to the hospital, Mr. Gornall said, "So valuable has the hospital been as a perfect means of isolation, that since the present powers came into force, there has been a most remarkable and satisfactory diminution in the death rate from this disease." From Mr. Whittle's remarks he took it that a diminution in the death rate was of no consequence to him compared to having money taken out of his pockets. Mr. Gornall went on to say—"ln the half-year of 1879, previous to the Act coming into force, there were sOme 34 deaths from scarlet fever, whilst in the latter half of the year there were only six," so that 28 lives had been saved. Mr. Whittle put a very small estimate upon human life, if he did net value them all round at £lO each. (Laughter.) He said nothing of the benefit to the head of a family who was struck down by disease and unable to follow his occupation, who could be sent to the hospital rather than to the workhouse if he was poor. That meant to say that it would save to the inhabitants of the town £BOO a year as far as doctors' fees were concerned. What would be the saving in other ways? The resolution for the adoption of the minutes of the Canal Boats and Hospital Committee was moved by Mr. LYON, and seconded by Mr. MEADOWCROFT. In reply to Mr. Haalehurst, Mr. HANDLEY said the com- mittee had had an interview with Mr. Beswick, Lord Choi- mondeley's agent, as to the erection of the infectious diseases hospital. On the following Wednesday morning Mr. Bestvick would stake out the land; and Mr. Barker had been ordered to have the plans prepared for the next meeting of the committee. He (Mr. Handley) had a matter to bring before the Board, which, although it did not arise on the minutes, he thought he was in order in bringing forward. It was that he saw from an account of the Daresbury Petty Sessions that the Commissioners were about to be reported to the Local Government Board as a defaulting authority in carrying out the Canal Boats' Act. From the fact that that Board was the first to take up the Act to try to work it properly; it reflected very much on them that such a course should have at all been suggested. The CHAIRMAN put the motion for the adoption of the minutes of the meeting, which was carried, and then gave Mr. Handley an opportunity of discussing the question he had introduced. Mr. BROOKES, secretary, produced the Canal Boats' Re- gister and Receipt Book at the request of Mr. Handley, and explained that the boat in question was examined on the 3rd January, and the report sent in to the meeting of the committee. The recommendation came before the Beard meeting of February 7th, and on that day the certificate of registration was made out and ready for the boatman to take away. Mr. MEADOWCROTT asked if it was a proper state of things that a whole month should elapse. Delay of this kind was very hard on owners of vessels. Mr. BROOKES stated that if application had been made to him for the certificate after he knew the boat had been ex- amined he should have granted him a clearance until the certificate could be issued, but no application was made to him until after the Board meeting on February 7th. . Dr. McDonaALL moved that the secretary should write to the magistrates' clerk asking...whether the newspaper report was substantially correct. If it was so, it would clearly be the duty of the Board to purge itself of a gross charge which had been made. There had been no fault on the part of the Commissioners, but rather an excess of zeal on part of the magistrates. Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN thought if the Board took notice of all newspaper reports they might give their servants con- stant employment. It would have been much better if the , consideration of the matter had been adjourned. Mr. HANDLEY : It was the word of the inspector, not the boatman, that was taken. ITTNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMIS- SIONERS. The monthly meeting was held on Monday. Mr. George Marshall presided, and there were also present Messrs Norman, Frith, Timmins, Handley, Shaw, Steele, Hanle- burst, J. J. Speakman, Meadowcroft, Williams, Lyon, Dob- son, McDougall. Linaker (law clerk), Brookes (secretary), Barker (surveyor), and Mouritz (medical officer.) MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. Mortara's report showed that the number of deaths registered during the past month was 20, representing a death rate of 17 per 1000 per annum. Of these eleven were due to whooping cough, four to bronchitis, and two to diseases of the nervous system. Dropsy, phthisis, and hepatic disease Accounted for one each. Twelve deaths occurred amongst children five years and under, and eight happened unde.. one year. Two inquests had been held, making the total deaths 22. The births numbered 52, or an average of 44 per 1000. Whooping cough had been epidemic in the district during the past month, and owing to the severe easterly winds, proved exceedingly fatal. THE NONCONFOR.MISTS AND CANON BARCLAY : TILE ALLEGED SECTARIAN JEALOUSY. Dr. MCDOUGALL moved that the Board should go into committee for the purpose of discussing the following com- munication from the Rev. Canon Barclay, MA. : The Vicarage, Runcorn. To the Chairman of the Finance Committee of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners. Brookes v Barclay. Dear Sir.—Although professionally advised that I have a good case if either the Commissioners or myself should appeal to a kigher court, yet to avoid expense, which. if incurred by the Commissioners, they would pay out of the public rates, but my share of which I should have to Px out of my own re- Sources, I beg respectfully to propose that the suggestion of the on the 21st inst., magistrates. made at the Petty 5e5410.9 should be adopted, viz., that under the provisions of the Public Health Act, 1875, sec. 150, the Commissioners should declare the expenses incurred in making Fox-street. and Eaton-street to be "private improvement expenses," and that, as empowered to do by the same Act, sec 213. they should allow the payment to extend over a term of 30 years. I make the latter request because, as my tenure of the benefice cannot now. in the natural course of things, be very long, it seems unfair that I should pay out of my own pocket a large sum of money for improvements of which my suecessors will reap the benefit. I have only to add that this offer is made without prejudice as regards the question either of ownership or liability, neither of which I admit.—l have the honour to remain, sir, yours respectfully, (Signed) JOHN BARCLAY. March 30th, 1881. The mover considered it desirable that the matter should be discussed in committee. - - The motion having been, seconded, Mr. SHAW remarked that he did not consider the proposal to resolve themselves into a committee of the whole Board a wise one, because if they did so, they would merely have to discuss the commu- nication from Canon Barclay twice, as it was referred to under the minutes of the Finance Committee. He should certainly have to refer to some remarks made by the Vicar of Runcorn in which certain members of the Board were charged with a grave irregularity. Whatever migkt be said in committee, he certainly should not, as far as he was con- cerned, permit it to be exclsively considered in private, as he was of opinion that as the statement of Canon Barclay had been made in public, its repudiation must also be in public. Mr. HaztEnunar said the reason for going into committee on the subject was that the case was pending its decision before the Runcorn magistrates that morning, and what they might do as the result of their discussion would pro- bably affect it in some way or other. Mr. Straw was of opinion that, if the statement of Mr. Hazlehurst was correct, it would be very undignified of that Board to take any steps which would interfere with a ques- tion that would be taken before the magistrates for decision. It would seem as if the Board did not do sometiug excep- tional such conduct might influence some decision else- where. Mr. HANDLEY considered that in the interests of the pub- lic they-ought not to go into committee on this question. He did not know whether the gentlemen who were propos- ing and seconding this discussion did not wish their remarks to made public. However, he thought there were mem- bers en the Board who were not afraid of expressing their opinions upon this question freely ; and, seeing that the case had excited a great deal of comment, both private and pub- lic—for he believed it had oeen quoted in a great many newspapers—the more public the discussion was and the- better it was fer the Commissioners. (Cries of hear, hear.) He, therefore, hoped the members of the Board would not lend themselves to any proposition which had for its object gagging the press and keeping the public out of information to which they were justly entitled. Mr. FRITH was of opinion that it would be undignified on the part ef the Commissioners, after the publicity which had been given to the observations of Canon Barclay, to resolve themselves into committee. The same publicity ought to be given to any remarks which were uttered there as to those which Canon Barclay had made when before the

doing anything in reference to the clai• m for improvement expenses from that gentleman which he should not have done in any other case. He felt sure that as far as his own conduct at that Board was concerned, it would bear the strictest investigation. He could only speak for himself, as a Nonconformist, in regard to the matter. In conclusion he might refer to what be considered about the greatest joke he had beard since he had been in the town, and that was that the Nonconformist ministers might discharge certain duties at the Cemetery, and the vicar of Runcorn should receive the fees. This he took as a great joke on the term " equity." Mr. HANDLEY said the Finance Committee was composed of both Nonconformists and Churchmen, and when the remarks made.by the vicar were spoken of at their meeting a general feeling was expressed that they were not applic- able to the Board of Commissioners. In fact, all through the progress of the matter the members of the committee had felt that, for the time being, they were entrusted with a very unpleasant duty, and one which might' lay them open to such a charge. They had, therefore, been careful all through the time the proceedings had been pending to avoid anything that would bear any semblance of sectarian in fact, simply carried out what the jealousy. They had, Act of Parliament told them to do; they had dispensed its provisions in their integrity, and, in fact,they had no choice but to do what they had done. If Canon Barclay had treated the Board with that consideration which even the Book from whence he professed to draw his lessons -of morality and religion should have taught him; if he had met the Board in that spirit, then no such complication as that with which they were then dealing would have arisen. So long as the Commissioners were the rulers of Runcorn, they ought to be treated with that courtesy which they deserved—altogetb er apart from their individual characters as men—and if the vicar had done so the present state of things could not possibly have arisen. Many persons, since reading the observOons of Canon Barclay, appeared to have the idea that the gentleman in question had tried to arrange the question in dispute with the Board. However, he might say that since Canon Barclay had appeared at the police court he had never recognised the Board of Cemmissioners- at all; and until there was some approach on that gentle- man's part it was impossible for them to do otherwise than they had done as custodians of the public purse- The Caatamew : Before putting the motion to the meeting I feel bound to make one statement. It has been my duty to attend every committee meeting and every meeting of the Board when this matter has been under discussion, and both personally and as Chairman of the Board I feel bound to state that there has not been the slightest manifestation of any personal feeling on the part of any member; and they have always exhibited a disposition to do what was honour- able to everyone. Mr. Noantes: I quite endorse everything that has been said, and I think that inasmuch as Dr. Steele and Mr. Lyon are members of Canon Barclay's congregation, it would be as well if they would say distinctly that they have never seen anything of sectarian jealousy. , The CHAIRMAN : No, no; you are out of order, Mr. Nor- Man. We cannot deal with that. Mr. NORMAN: I think they might distinctly say that they have never seen anything like sectarian jealousy. Dr. Smema said the discussion seemed almost tantamount to asking Canon Barclay to make an apology; but from what bad been said it looked very much as if the cap fitted somewhere. (Cries of "No, no.") Mr. Straw: Will Dr. Steele accept the cap, then? (Laughter.) Mr. Dossoar wished to know whether he was right in sup- posing that the case was now a question of litigation. The CHAIRMAN: I think that we can scarcely answer that question this morning. Mr. DOBSON (anxiously) : I really think that something should be done to prevent the ratepayers' money being spent in litigation. The CHAIRMAN: I think that is a matter for the commit- tee to consider. Mr. HANDLEY : But we have not lost the case. The Bench expressed no opinion as to legality or illegality of the claim. The LAW CLERE : They gave a verdict for the defen- dant ! Mr. Tnottais was of opinion that, as the matter had been fought, it would now be better to let it drop. Mr. LINAYER said there was another question to be con- sidered : What would the auditor say to the collector when he came at the end of the year? He would not be content with the ruling of the Bench, and would sur- charge the Board. M. NORMAN: Yes, somebody will be in for it. Mr. SHAW said the auditor would be guided by the law, which said that if there was a church on the land for which ' Canon Barclay had been charged for street making it would be exempt. The law did not say anything about land set apart for the erection of a place of worship, it simply re- ferred:to buildings. RtNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIAN 3.

At the fortnightly meeting of this Board, held on Tuesday, at the Workhouse, Dutton, Mr. John,Ashton (vice-chairman) occupied the chair, and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. 'fanner, Messrs. T. Norman, R. Ashton, H. Lowe, W. Whitlow, W. Pickering, J. Darbyshire, H. Neild, P. Percival, P. Briscoe, G. S. Hazlehurst, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).

body of William Grice, aged 53, a labourer employed by Mr. Kirkham, contractor at the Widnes Alkali Works, who was killed on the iron railway bridge (L. and N. W.) near the Marsh, on Saturday aftersoon. Mr. Ferrant, from the solicitors department, Lime-street station, watched the case on behalf of the railway company. Ann Grice, widow of deceased, said she lived in Sewell- street, Runcom, and her husband left home to go to his work on Saturday morning, about half past four. John Welsby Ellison, a chemical works' labourer, in the same employ as deceased, said on Saturday a little before one o'clock, he left the works, and walked home along the St. Helens canal. Deceased was a few yards behind him. When witness got to the iron bridge an engine with seven wagons was approaching very slowly. Deceased was about 40 or 60 yards behind witness, who ran across the line. On looking round he saw deceased lying under the fifth wagon from the engine. He called out to the engine driver, who stopped the engine, and witness and another man went to the deceased, whom they found quite dead. The wheels had gone across the chest of deceased. Information was given to the police and the body taken to the Commercial Inn. Witness and deceased were in the habit of going across the bridge from their work. Witness had never gone home by any other way during the time he had been employed at the Alkali Works. It was a regular practice of the men to go that way. They had no authority from the railway company to cross the line, but they had never been stopped by any of the company's servants. There was no one to blame except deceased himself. He was of opinion that deceased, think- ing the train was stopped, crept between the wagons in order to overtake his companions. It would have taken about a minute to have gone round the train. The engine driver gave no signal before he started. The pointsraan never told either him or deceased to stop. The Foreman: Is there a right of way across the bridge ? Mr. Ferrand : They have no right there at all. A Juryman: Yes, there is a right of way. There has been one for thirty years. Several other gentlemen stated that to their knowledge there was a right of way across the bridge in question to the Marsh. Mary °Ann Stokes, said she saw deceased stooping, as though to get under some wagons of a train which was on the bridge. The wheel caught him on the shoulder, turned him over, and three wagons passed across his shoulder, leav- ing him lying with his face aciess the line. One of the wagons was thrown off the rails owing to the accident. Witness, who was about 20 yards away, said it was while the wagons were in motion that deceased attempted to creep through. She did not hear the driver sound the whistle, nor could she say whether the train stood at all prior to the deceased attempting to get undet the wagon. George Lawrinson, driver of the locomotive,deposed that, while shunting on the sidings near the canal bridge, he noticed some persons cross about 20 or 40 yards in front of the engine. When the engine got across the bridge it just stopped, but not for more than a second, when be reversed and went back. He did not whistle before he opened the regulator. The Coroner: I thought it was your duty before you re- versed the regulator, to open the whistle. Witness said they could not pretend to do so every shunt. If they did so they might keep the whistle open altogether He looked down the train to see that all was clear, but he. did not perceive anybody about. Directly after he had re- versed the engine, he noticed one of the waggons jump. At first he thought one of them had left the rails until he heard the witness Ellison and some other men shout. He immediately stopped the engine, and the body was removed. He was sure the waggons never stood still. Workmen were continually crossing the bridge. Wm. Collier, a shunter, corroborated the evidence of the last witness. James Tomlinson, a young man, who has charge of the bridge, was also examined. He said he had been employed to look after the bridge for about three weeks. He had no instructions to stop persons from crossing. He had cau- tioned people about going underneath the waggons while standing on the bridge. John Stott, foreman shunter, said he was about ten yards away from the bridge when the accident happened. He had been foreman shunter about nine years, and the public had been in the habit of using this bridge all that time. He had no instructions to stop them. They were in the habit of passing under the waggons when in motion. They "popped" under, notwithstanding the cautions given them. A Juryman remarked that it was an every day occurrence. The Coroner said it wae only too evident how the unfor- tunate man had come to his death. He bad been attempting to pass under the wagons while they were in motion, and had been knocked down and killed instantly. It was quite clear that the wagons were never stationary for a single moment. A very important question had been raised as to the right of the public to cross the bridge, but that did not affect the verdict for the reason that, supposing it was a public level crossing, people ought to exercise ordinary care. If people were so foolish as to run the risk of attempting to pass under wagons while they were in motion, the company could not be _held responsible. It was, however, very de- sirable that it should be ascertained whether the public had a right of way or not. If they bad not, then some decisive step should be taken to stop trespassers. If the public had a right of way, then they ought to be be secured from the dangers which at present exist. No one was to blame except the unfortunate man himself; therefore, there was no other course open to them but to return a verdiet of accidental death. If they wished, they could add a present- ment, calling the attention of the company to the state of the crossing and as to the future regulation of the traffic. The Jury expressed an opinion that there was a public right of way across the swing bridge to and from- the works and other property on the Marsh, and that the present dangerous state of the crossing called for some public action. The Coroner pointed out that they could not censure the railway company if it was private property. The company were not bound to protect trespassers. He, however, was strongly of opinion that something ought to be done to ascertain whether it was a public road or not. He suggested that a public meeting should be called, or that the Local Board should be memorialised upon the subject. He hoped something would be done, as the matter was at present in a most unsatisfactory state. No doubt the publicity that would be given to the o2inions expressed at that inquiry would cause some action to be taken with regard to the I matter. The Jury returned a veict of "Accidental death."

when poverty came in at the door love very often went out of the window. Let yonng men spend less on drink and tobacco. Although a young man might be poor, if he were steady success was sure to crown his efforts. Taking it for .granted that some of them present were married, he would give a few hints on home life. First, the) must not expect too much. Some people imagined that to be married was to be in heaven at once. The raarriage state bad been com- pared to a a lottery, in which there were many blanks and but few prizes. The advice be had to give them was " keep on courting." Too many thought that at the wedding all the attentions paid during courtship must cease. Before marriage, if Mary Jane dropped her handkerchief, the lover was quite proud to be allowed to pick it up, or to pay any little attention to his chosen one, bat often after marriage a great change took place. Sone married men walked out in advance of their wives with a look on their faces as if to say, "No connection with the woman behind." (Laughter.) In his opinion, the husband should be as anxious to please after as before marriage. If this were done, home life in many cases would be very different from what it was. The ,wife should recognise the lordship of her husband, and the husband should recognise the equality of his wife. He also advised married people to reverence the Sabbath, and teach their children to honour the Bible by reading it. It was also the duty of the husband to keep and protect his wife. Many men cared more for clothing the landlady than their own wives. As far as they could, they should surround their wives with comforts, and always remember " the old love." Some men seemed to think that their wives were made to be their slaves; but this ought not to be so. Woman was not made out of man's head, to be above him ; neither was she made out of his foot to be trampled upon by him ; but she was made out of a rib from his side, and near his heart, to be loved by, and on an equality with him. It was the duty of wives to be submissive to their husbands, but many women, no sooner were they married, than they defied their husbands. A Frenchman speaking at a public meeting said there was a woman in the audienee who had disobeyed her husband that day, and in order to point her out he would throw a book at her head. It was recorded that every woman present held her head down to escape being struck. (Laughter.) Many a man would be a better husband if his home were kept a little more comfortable for him, and it should be the wife's aian to make it„, bright and pleasant. But there was a home to which earthly homes could not be compared. Neither sickness nor death could damp its joys; and he earnestly hoped that they would all prepare themselves for this their eternal home in heaven.

div.head: LETTER FROM THE CHAIRMAN.
div.p: LETTER FROM THE CHAIRMAN.

The Chairman (the Rev. Canon Barclay) wrote from Penmaenmaur that, having had to escort his wife to that place for a change of air, and being over persuaded to stay for a few days, he would not be at the Board on Tuesday. He was sorry to be absent, as he believed it was the last meeting of the present Board, and perhaps the Clerk would be kind enough to express for him his grateful sense of the courtesy which the Guardians had shown to himself per- sonally, and the readiness with which they had on every occasion supported the authority of t,e chair. The letter concluded with most'heartily wishing the retiring members happiness and prosperity in private life.

div.head: . . THE DUSTER'S REPORT.
div.p: . . THE DUSTER'S REPORT.

The Master's report, stated that the number of inmates was 164 as against 157 in the corresponding week in last year. There had been 4 men, 2 women, and 1 child vagrants relieved during the week. There were in atten- dance at the workhouse school 20 boys and 27 girls ; and 10 boys and 20 girls were receiving industrial training. Out- door relief had been administered to 606 persons, at a cost of £6l 7s. 2d. (Runcorn £34 ss. 6d., Frodsham £l4 9s. 2d., Budworth £l2 12s. 64.) as compared with 699 persons re- lieved at a cost of £66 19s. 3d. in the corresponding week in last year.

THE INFIRMARY ACCOMMODATION. A letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated 26th March, as follows f—" I am directed by the Local Government to advert to your letter of the 11th ult., forwarding plans of the proposed additional infirmary ac- commodation at the Runcorn Union Workhouse, and to state that the Board have caused the plans to be examined by their architect, Mr. P. G. Smith, and they are advised by him that the plans are capable of amendment in -certain points of detail men- tioned in the enclosed architectural notes. The plans are returned herewith, and I am directed to request that the suggestions contained in the notes may receive the conside- ration of the Guardians, and that the plans may be amended in accordance therewith and re-transmitted to the Board." Mr. LOWE : How many times is this the plans have been returned? Mr. NORMAN: It is the first time these have been returned. The Visiting Committee have had the plans before them, and recommend an alteration that will satisfy the Local Government Board. On the motion of the Rev. J. W. N. TANNER, the plans were ordered to be transmitted as requested.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICIALS. A letter was read from the Local Government Board, sanctioning the payment of the sum of £35 to the Clerk for his services to the School Attendance Committee during the year. The Board also approved the appointment, to the 25th May, 1882, of Messrs. Wright, Thomas Riley, and Wm. It. de Prez, as the school attendance officers, and sanctioned the payment of £22 10s. to Messrs. Riley and de Prez, and £l2 lOs per annum to Mr. Wright, for their services during the period for which they have been appointed. A CONTRACT-CANCELLED. • Mr. W. HANDLEY, of Runcorn, wrote to say that as he understood he had been elected a Guardian for the Union, he had to ask the Board to cancel the contract he had entered into for the supply of boots and shoes. On the proposition of Mr. NORMAN, the contract was can- celled. FINANCE COMMITTEE. Mt. NORMAN stated that the Finance Committee had gone very carefully through the accounts which amounted to £749 14s. 6d.

_ THE ELECTION EXPENSES. On the motion of Mr. NORMAN, the Clerk was voted the sum of £l5 remuneration for his services as returning officer for the elections. ABOLITION OF THE OFFICE OF OVERSEER. The copy of a memorial from the Salford Union praying for the abolition of the office of overseer of the poor was laid before the Board. The memorial stated the memorialists were of opinion that a great saving would be effected by abolishing the office and referring the duties of collection and distribution to the otker collecting authorities—Town Councils, Local Boards, and Guardians. It was anticipated that smaller bank balances would suffice, and a saving would be effected in the cost of collecting and office expenses, thus leading to a diminution of the rates. A committee was appointed to consider the circular and report to the Board. . RETIREMENT OF AN OLD GUARDIAN.

He enjoy the rest and retirement which he had so well earned. The CHAIRMAN: Has he retired, then? Mr. PERCIVAL : Yes, be has. Rev. J. W. TANNER had great pleasure in seconding the proposition. He did not know a worthier member of the Board than Mr. Baxter. He had been a member for 18 years, and they had looked upon him as a man they could depend upon for sound advice. He thought as a body they thoroughly respected him, and he hoped their vote would be unanimous. Mr. PERCIVAL He has been a member of the Assessment Committee ever since it was formed, and a very useful member Mr. Baxter has been. The CHAIRMAN said, in putting the proposition, he. was very sorry Mr. Baxter had retired. He could say that Mr. Baxter had been a very good member. He had known him for something like 10 or 12 years, during which he had been a guardian, and during the whole of that time he had always looked upon him as an efficient member. The proposition was carried. VOTES OF THANKS. The CHAIRMAN proposed a vote of thanks to the Chair- man of the Board (the Rev. Canon Barclay) for his services during the year. He had always guided them aright, and they had always managed to get on with the business in a very efficient manner. He was sorry that the Chairman was not there that day to receive their thanks, but they had a letter from him explaining why he could not attePd, and he was sure the resolution that he had proposed would meet with their cordial approval. Mr. NORMAN had great pleasure in seconding the proposi- tion, as he thought Canon Barclay this last year had been the right man in the right place. The proposition was carried unanimously. Rev. J. W. N. TANNER thought they would be sadly re- miss if they did not pass a similar vote of thanks to the Vice-Chairman. He had attended very regularly, and in the absence of the chairman had well filled his place. His courteoui manner, and the way in which he had carried on the business of the Board, ought to be commended, and, therefore, he had the greatest possible pleasure in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Ashton. Mr. PICKERING seconded the motion, which was carried without dissent. , The CHAIRMAN, in reply, gaid it had always been a pleasure to hi.n to preside in the absence of the Rev. Canon Barclay. Mr. ROBERT ASHTON proposed a vote of thanks to the Clerk, and hoped he would long be spared to occupy the office. Mr. PERCIVAL seconded, and Mr. NORMAN supported the motion. He thought it was the first time he had ever heard of such a thing at the Board, and he did think the Clerk deserved their thanks as much as anyone. (Hear, hear.) They never seemed to get into trouble, as other people did—either financially or in any other way—and he thought the way the business was con- ducted in connection with that Union was' not equalled by any other. The proposition was heartily carried.
THE -REV. HENRY VALENTINE, OF RUNCORN, ON. COURTSHIP AND MARRIAGE.

Gamon, and there were present on the platform the Rev. Mr. Bateman, and Messrs. A. Davies, R. Hughes, W. Jukes, and J. Looker. The Rev. H. VALENTINE delivered a lecture On "Home, sweet hem?.; or, plain talk about courtship and marriage." He said the word " home " entered into all friendly associa- tions. Of course the young man had a reason for, liking the young woman. ome married dimples, others noses, and many married money. Who need wonder, under such a state of things, that so many marriages turned out badly ? He would say let the wife be a woman the man could love, but love must not be the only reason for man iage. div.head: LECTURE ON GEOLOGY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: LECTURE ON GEOLOGY AT RUNCORN.

A lecture was delivered in St. John's schoolroom on Wednesday evening, by Mr. Wm. Leach. The subject was " Geology—a glance over the past ages of the earth's his- tory." The chair was occupied by the Rev. R. Williams, who very briefly introduced the lecturer.—Mr: Leach said tbere were thousands who walked the earth for years who knew little more about its composition when they passed off it than when they Came upon it. Perhaps many of them were not aware that they were walking over the graves of thousands of beings who"' were now entombed in the rocks. The theory that the earth had only been in existence a few thous And years was not a true one ; we lived in a very old world. He could trace back to a period when there was DO life whatever in the earth. It was supposed that at one time the globe was in a state of vapour or gas, which, having a rotary motion, gradually condensed into a fiery mass of matter. This was the period when granite was the result of fire. The earth still cooling, the vapouis which surrounded it fell down upon it in the form of water and, covered the whole world, which was submerged for ages. The action of tiiie water, as it rose and fell in tides, in the process of time formed the stratified rocks. There was also another kind of rock, which had been formed by I he combined actions of fire and water. To this latter class marble belonged. It was composed of other rocks, which had been by some agency ground down to a fine powder. The next kind of ' rock to be mentioned was the Cambrian, so called because a great deal of it was found in Wales. It was in this rock that the first evidence of life was discovered. The creatures found in this rock had no eyes, thus clearly proving that at this period of the earth's history it was in darkness. 25,000 feet higher, in the next layer of rock, they found what they supposed to be the most perfect creatures ever made. They had no back bone, but could roll up into a ball, in which position ' many of them were now found. There were thousands of them to be seen in this kind of rock. The layers of rock were always seen in their proper order, unless by the action of some mighty agency they had been thrown one on another. It was only in this way that they could account for the granite sometimes being found on the surface. The earth had undergone many violent convulsions; had been rent and torn by some great.force—probably fire, and it was in this way that the mountains had been formed. This was clearly proved by the fact that many of the rocks were discovered with the strata in a position which was originally horizontal, hut which was no, perpendicular. Time would not permit of his going any further into the subject, or he might have spoken of ' how coal ame to exist, but he would recommend all to look up the subject for themselves, as he was quite sere they would find it interesting and beneficial. It W:l5 a subject in which time wisdom and handiwork of God were clearly dis- played. At the close a collection was made in aid of the school expenses, after which the usual vote of thanks were Passed, and the proceedings terminated.
