div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY.—Before Mr. George Pillcington. A COVPLE OF ALLEGED POCKET PICKER/ CAIMIT.— James Stephens and Mary Tearney were brought up, on remand, charged with having stolen from the person of . .

, Bridget Ryan, th'e sum of 11s:8d. and one pawnticket ; and also stolen a purse, seven pawntickets, and £3 14s. ed., be- longing to Mrs. Higgins.—Mrs. Ryan, wife of Martin Ryan, of Charlotte-street, said that on the 19th ult., about half-

past seven in the evening, she was on the Widnes market ground, watching a woman who was selling earthenware. Whilst there she felt in her pocket and found her purse and money safe. The female prisoner came to her and began a conversation by talking to witness's child. She noticed that the woman rubbed against her, and pulled her dress, and the male prisoner was standing near to them, and trying to draw off their attention from his companion by telling them she was his mother, and at one time in the pot trade, when he acted as auctioneer for her. They remained close to her about ten minutes, and then the female prisoner started off, speaking to the child as she left. The male prisoner fol- lowed, and joined her at the corner of the Market Hall. Witness went home, where she felt for her purse to get money to pay for some beer, when she found it and the money and pawnticket gone. She gave information to the police, and on Sunday she was taken to the police station and shown a number of prisoners, out of whom she picked the two then in the dock as being the couple she had seen near her on the market ground.—Ellen Twigg, wife of James Twigg, of 71, John-street, gave evidence to the effect that she was with the last witness on the night of the robbery, and she saw the female prisoner pull Mrs. Ryan's dress. This proceeding attracted her attention, and she told a woman named Mrs. Snelson, who was with her.—Mrs. enelson said she saw the female prisoner hold of the prosecutrix's dress, and pulled her own purse out of her pocket and kept it in her hand.—Ellen, wife of Patrick Hig- gins, of Margaret-street, Widnes, said that on Saturday, the 19th ult., she was at a butcher' tall in the market ground buying some meat. The female prisoner came and stood partly behind her as she had her purse in her left band pay- ing for the meat. The woman leaned over her and saw what she was doing. After paying what she owed she put her purse in her right hand dress pocket, and it contained .£3 14s. 6d.. and seven pawn tickets. At this time the male prisoner stood close behind the female prisoner, aid they afterwards walked away together. She went towards home, and as she was doing so the female prisoner stepped in front of her, put her hand upon her shoulder, and made some remark as to the price she had paid for meat. The woman I then rubbed her hand down her right side and said she had no right to pay such a price as she had done. Witness then went up Caroline-street, and at the botsom of that thorough- fare felt in her pocket and found her purse, which contained the money, ditc., missing. No one had been near her since she paid for the meat but the female prisoner. She went on to Anne-street, and on her way heard the two prisoners talking and laughing together. She gave information to the police, who found the couple in a lodging-bouse in Elizabeth-street about midnight. On the following day she was shown the stolen puree and pawn tickets.—Franis Keat- ing;ll4 years of age, of Major Cross-street, said that on the date in question he was assisting at the butcher's stall where the prosecutrix bought the meat, and saw the prisoners near her. The female prisoner had her hand near the prosecu- trix, who, after leaving the stall, came back to complain she had been robbed.—Mr. Mason, manager to the proprietor of the Market Hotel, said that on the night of the robbery the two prisoners came to the house, and the female one ordered ale, for which she paid with a sovereign.—James Wright, labourer, 16, Pool-street, said that on Sunday, the 20th March, he found the stolen purse and the seven pawn tickets produced, at about half-past nine in the morning, on a window sill at the WAlevan schools, Lacey-street, and he gave them to P.C. Stott.—The last-named officer gave evi- dence as to going to the lodging-house where the prisoners were staving and apprehending them, in the presence of the prosecutrix, who said they were the people who had robbed her.—P.C. Pitt said that on apprehending the female prisoner she took out of her purse £2 12s. sp., and said that on the previous night she received the money from her hush md.— Prisoners, who denied having anything to do with the rob- bery, were committed for trial to the Liverpool Quatter Sessions.

MotuAv.—Before Mr. George Pilkington. THE JOINER AND HIS RE6oTIVES.—JaMeS Lee, aged 33, was brought up on remand from the previous Friday charged with having, on the 7th May, 1879, stolen £lO and two silver watches, value £l2 10s., the property of George Fountain, greengrocer, Anne-street, West, under circum- stances fully reported in last week's Examiner. The prisoner, who obtained the assistance of the prosecutor, on the representation that he was his wife's cousin, and had just come from America, denied his guilt,and was committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. George Pi I kin gton THE STREET OBSTRUCTION NUISANCE. Michael Riley, Patrick Riley, Michael Minna, and James Fancy, were sun's moned for unlawfully obstructing the free passage of Waterloo-road, by standing, thereon and refusing to move when requested to de so by a police officer.—P.C. Pitt said that about a quarter to eleven, on the night of the 26th ult., he saw the four defendants standing in Waterloo-road, and causing an obstruction, so that people had to leave the foot- path. He asked them to go away, but they would not do so.—Mr. l'ilkington said the case was not a very serious one, , but the peactice of which the defendants had been guilty was a very objectionable one.—Each of the defendants would be fined is. and Gs. od. costs. THREATENING A WATERLOO-ROAD DRAPER. Mr. WITI. King, who is in business in Waterloo-road, was summoned for having, on the 30th ult., used threatening language t”- wards Mr. Wm. Miller, draper.—Mr. Husband appeared for the complainant, and stated that defendant was Mr. Miller's brother-in-law. On the 31st ult., he went into the com- plainant's shop, used some very strong adjectives,. and threatened to knock his head off.—Complainant gave evi- dence in support of this statement, and it was corroborated by P.C. Thom John Jones, an errand boy, and Mr. Miller's assistant, John Sandland.—Defendant said he put Mr. Miller in busineSs, and he had had "no end of trouble' with him. He had also been much provoked by com- plainant causing quarrels between himself and his wife, Defendant was ordered to be hound over in the sum of £2O, and two sureties in £lO each, to keep the peace to com- plainant for 12 months.

COXGREGATIONAL SCHOOLS, OVEIL—In connection with the opening of the new Sunday school a service of song, entitled "Robert Raikes," was given in the school-room on Thursday. The choir rendered their part well. The atten- dance was very discouraging. We understand the service iS to he repeated, when, it is to be hoped, the efforts of the pro- moters will be repaid by a better attendance.

DEATEL AND BURIAL OP ME. SAMUEL TAYLOR.—It iS with regret we have to record the death of Mr. Samuel Tay- lor, of Ecclestod Hall, who died op. Monday morning. Mr. Taylor recently made an offer of a park to the town, and he was then known to be in an infirm state of health, Mr. Taylor for flunk years suffered from a chronic complaint, and a cataract delAved him of the use of his eyes About four years age. A surgical, operation was, however, per- formed, and his sight partially restored. He was always fend of horse riding, and freely indulged this fancy up to a few months ago, being almost daily on horse back. He was the oldest magistrate in the district, was 79 years of age, and leaves three sons, two of whom are clergymen, and the youngest a solicitor in Manchester. The funeral took place on Thursday morning in a quiet manner. The body was Interred at Christ Church, Eccieston. The Rev.. Crockett impressively read the Burial Sery im,ces, and a ereg( number of friends and neighbours witnessed the solemn pro- ceedings.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, at the offices, Bridgewater-street. Mr. John Simpson, vice-chair- man, presided, and there were also present Rev. Father Fennelly, Messrs. Norman, Pritchard, Lea, Briscoe, and Rigby- (clerk).

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE RETURNS.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE RETURNS.

The usual monthly report, presented by Mr. Bowyer, showed :—Certified Government accommodation, 2,289; number on the rolls, 2,719; average attendance, 1,851.9; average attendance for March, 1880, 1.9114; average attendance for the year 1874, 1,252; accommodation in ex- cess of average attendance, 437 1 ; the number on the rolls in excess of accommodation was 430. There was a decrease in the average attendance, compared with the corresponding pniod of last year, of 595, and an increase, as compared with 1874, the year preceding the formation of the Board, of 1600. The total number in attendance at private adventure I schools under ninepence per week was 53. The decrease in the average attendance was principally in the infant schools, caused by the inclement weather and whooping cough, which had boen prevalent.

div.head: IMPORTANT MINUTES.
div.p: IMPORTANT MINUTES.

The minutes of the ordinary and special meeting were read by the clerk. The last named meeting was held for the purnese of meeting Mr. George Holme, the architect to the Board, in order to instruct him as to the wishes of the Board in preparing rough plans of a proposed new school for 500 children, and to point out to him the various sites which had , been considered eligible and recommended by the Sites Com- mittee. In reply to enquiries from several members of the Board, Mr. HOLISM stated that a school of two storeys might be advantageous both as regarded cost and convenience, but that a three storey building would be less convenient and no cheaper than a two story building. The Board, with the architect, then visited Albert-street, which was pronounced by him to be a good site for one school of 250 children but not large enough for 500. The site at the lower end of Greenway-road, recommended by the committee, was also pronounced to be a good one ; but it was resolved that the site of the Land Company adjoining the Cemetery off Greenway-road was the most suitable. It was ordered that the clerk communicate with the Land Company respecting the site, and that upon re- ceiving a plan of land from them, together with its price, he instructed the architects to the Board to prepare rough plans for a school for 500 children. The minutes were approved. _

' Education Department, 2nd April, 1891.--81r,—Adverting to your letter of the 2nd February, I am directed to inquire whether your Board have yet succeeded in obtaining a site for the required new school, art d whether they can submit plans providing for 100 boys an lot/ glrls for the approval of the Department. —I have the honour to be, your obedient servant, P. Crum The CLERK said that the Board would not be justified in paying anything to the Land Company beyond the or- dinary expenses of vendor and vendee, asit was not proposed to make the purchase under compulsory powers. As to the Education Department's letter, he said it appeared the body in London wished to force upon the Board a school cr, the Albert-street side of the town, and one in Halton-road, and what the members of the School Board wished to do was simply to have a central school, and correspondence on the subject had been going on with the Education I epartment for two or three years. The first thing they would have to do would be to get the appproval 6,f the Education Depart- ment to what they proposed to do. If the members could ' show the Department that the site the School Board wished to admit was the most eligible one, they might come to their way of thinking, even though they had opposed it for three years. RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. MOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that JOHN DOLBY, 11 Esq.. District Auditor, will attend at the Commissioners' Offices, Bridg.e-street, Runcorn. at Ten o'clock in the Forenoon, on Monday, the 25th instant, for the purpose of Auditing the Accounts of the said Commissioners for the year ending March 25th, 1881; and Notice is hereby Further Given, that the said accounts will be deposited in the office of the said Commission- ers, and be open to the inspection of all persons interested for seven clear days before the said audit. W. BROOKES, Secretary to the said Commissioners. April 7th, 1881.

JOHN CHADWICK, DECEASED. PURSUANT to an Act of Parliament made and passed in the 22nd and 23rd years of the reign of Her present Majesty, cap. 35, hatituled " An Act to further amend the law of property and to relieve trustees," NOTICE IS HERSEY GIVEN; .that all Creditors and persons having any CLAIMS or DEMANDS upon or against the estate of the said JOHN CHAD WICK, fate of Haydock and Blackpool, both in the county of Lancaster, colliery proprietor, mining engineer and surveyor (who died on the Seventh day of October, 1880, and whose Will bearing date the Thirteenth day of July, 1880, was proved by Charles Edward Hindley, Thomas Turnbull, and Richard Chadwick, three of the executors therein named, on the Seventeeth day of December, 1880, in the Disuict Registry at Liverpool, of the Probate Division of Her Majesty's High Court of Justice), are hereby requded to send in the particulars of their claims or demands to us, the undersigned, on or before the Twentieth day of May next; and notice is hereby further given that after that day the said Executors will proceed to distribute the assets of the deceased among the parties entitled thereto, having regard to the claims of which the said Executors shall then have had notice, and that they will not be liable for the assets or any part thereof so distributed to any person of whose debt or claim they shall not then have had notice.—Dated the Sixth day of April, 1881. ROBERT DAVIES, SHARP. AND KIRKOONNEL, Solicitors for the said Executors. Market Place, Warrington.

MAKINSON AND WILCOCK, in returning their sincere thanks to their numerous patrons and the public generally for the very kind and liberal support they leave hitherto received, hope, by strict attention to the interests of their clients, and the piompt and faithful discharge of their duties, to continue to merit the same; the more so, as they are able to offer ad- vantages not generally enjoyed by those engaged in the same business, Mr. Makinson having had from early youth practical experience of the English Timber, Stone and Building Trades, and of Farming in all its branches, being at the present time a farmer himself on a large scale and, in addition, having served his apprenticeship to the ENGINEERING and MG,Lwarnmr busi- ness, besides having bad, during the last TEN years, consider- able practice its Valuing and Selling Colliery, Quarry, and other Machinery and Working Plant, Growing and Fallen Timber, Farming Stocks, Growing and Gathered Produce, Stocks-in- Trade, Household Furniture Innkeepers' Effects, Houses, Buildings, Landed Estates and Property generally, and also in cases involving Damage and Trespass. Mr. WILCOCK, also, has had the advantage of being brought up to Farming, together with that of having served an appren- ticeship to an eminent Veterinary Burgeon, combined with the experience he has had since his connection with this firm, enables him to give judicious and valuable advice in all cases in which he may be consulted. In conclusion, M. and W. beg their friends and the public generally to note that they have a trustworthy and efficient staff of assistants in their employ, who have been carefully trained to watch over the interests of those who favour the firm with their patronage; whilst last, but not least, their system of advertising, and the facilities they possess of ensuring an extensive circulation, enable them to offer the utmost pos- sible publicity to any sales entrusted to their management.
